#### Required staff, missionary, and visitor experience

The staff surface should remain one quiet page, not a wizard:

1. **What supporters see now** — current address, reach, page title/alias,
   new-Giving state, and a real responsive visitor preview.
2. **What changed** — the source event and effective/as-of time in plain
   language; no raw provider or database codes by default.
3. **What should supporters see?** — only currently eligible outcome cards,
   with the safest reversible outcome recommended. If staff reasonably expect
   an unavailable move option, one concise "Why can't I move this page?"
   disclosure names the missing same-purpose or recurring proof.
4. **What this will and will not do** — a four-row summary for Page, New gifts,
   Existing recurring gifts, and Search/shared links. This is the authoritative
   consequence summary; the visual preview supplements rather than replaces
   text.
5. **Complete** — exact buttons such as `Keep page`, `Publish transition page`,
   `Move this address`, or `Remove this address`. Only the last two require one
   final confirmation. The confirmation names the old route and exact target or
   removal consequence, focuses the cancel/least-destructive action, traps and
   restores keyboard focus correctly, and preserves the user's selection if
   reproof fails.

After success, the interface moves focus to a clear result heading and exposes
the result through an accessible status message. On mobile it uses a
single-column order, full-width touch targets, no hover-only explanations, and
no sticky action bar that obscures keyboard focus. Color and icons never carry
the lifecycle meaning alone.

Missionary contributors receive a read-only, plain-language summary and visitor
preview through their existing page workspace; they are not asked to resolve
SEO, financial, or recurring work. Visitors get exactly one honest result:
current page, substantive transition/information page, one-hop same-page move,
or true privacy-safe `404`. Removed pages may offer ordinary site navigation and a
separately labelled organization contact or general-giving link when D7 permits
it, but never an automatic redirect or inherited Designation.

#### Amendments required in the final C-prime-R wording

The final formulation should additionally bind all of the following:

- replace "informational page only after applicable transition coverage is
  complete" with a **coverage-state-aware informational or transition page**
  whose claims are independently proof-gated and through-dated;
- pin every permanent move directly to one already released, currently
  eligible immutable target route generation; forbid redirect chaining and
  quarantine the old route safely if that exact target later becomes
  ineligible;
- drop untrusted query strings and fragments by default, retaining only
  allowlisted revalidated attribution that cannot select a Designation,
  successor, locale, return path, or other routing behavior;
- use one tenant-branded real `404` plus `noindex` for every tombstone, with no
  Phase 22 `410` surface or public history oracle, and promise neither faster
  search removal nor completion of any external cleanup;
- require one activation/effect manifest covering origin response, scoped cache
  invalidation, internal links, canonical metadata, structured data, social
  metadata, and sitemap membership, while keeping every external observer
  non-authoritative;
- require the one-page, consequence-first, mobile and keyboard accessible UX
  above, with a single confirmation only for hard-to-reverse move/removal and
  no recurring manual certification for healthy routes.

### 21.9 Ruthless synthesis and binding path forward

The initial C-prime was directionally right but unsafe in four places. It waited
too long to permit an honest transition notice; allowed a different Page
identity to receive an automatic permanent redirect; let hidden scope dimensions
weaken public-URL uniqueness; and introduced an unnecessary public `410`
distinction. The ratified design fixes all four: a transition notice may publish
while financial or recurring work remains open but states only proved through-
dated facts; `308` is reserved for the same immutable Page identity receiving a
new canonical Listed-public route; the external namespace is uniquely Site ×
locale × canonical path; and every tombstone returns the same real privacy-safe
`404` plus `noindex`.

Implementation must proceed in this order:

1. establish the versioned path canonicalizer, reserved-path rules, exact public-
   namespace uniqueness, complete composite scope, immutable Route Generation,
   never-reused tombstone, and server-only grants;
2. implement one append-only disposition command with D2-head CAS, deterministic
   locking, exact final reproof, semantic idempotency, and an outbox-backed Route
   Effect Manifest;
3. make the Phase 5 request boundary run a fresh route/safety guard before any
   immutable cached payload, resolve one hop, recheck the target, drop untrusted
   parameters, redirect only navigation-safe `GET`/`HEAD`, and distinguish
   stable `200`/`308`/`404` from transient no-store `503`;
4. compose the one-page staff consequence review and read-only contributor
   summary from those exact domain results, never from editable HTTP or SEO
   controls;
5. migrate only after a complete Tenant/Site/locale/path census and production-
   shaped shadow resolution prove collision-free exact mappings; and
6. certify races, retries, repeated moves, target withdrawal, cache and metadata
   effects, privacy concealment, accessibility, production-volume lookup, and
   append-only recovery before any route becomes authoritative.

This is the smallest complete design: four plain user outcomes, one command
path, one rebuildable current projection, and no tenant-authored lifecycle or
redirect language.

### 21.10 Current Supabase, PostgreSQL, Next.js, and repository proof

- Supabase's current
  [Data API security guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api)
  and
  [RLS guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)
  require explicit privileges in addition to RLS, warn that views can bypass RLS
  unless deliberately protected, reject user-editable metadata as authorization
  truth, and state that service credentials may bypass RLS. D8 therefore keeps
  route/evidence/outbox tables in an unexposed operational schema, revokes
  `PUBLIC`/`anon`/`authenticated`, omits Realtime, and treats RLS as indexed
  defense in depth rather than the only server-command guard.
- Supabase's 2026
  [Data API default-exposure change](https://supabase.com/changelog?types=breaking-change)
  improves new-table defaults but is not a durable authorization contract. D8
  records explicit grants and negative role/function tests so an environment or
  platform-default change cannot expose route history.
- Supabase's current
  [RLS performance guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/troubleshooting/rls-performance-and-best-practices-Z5Jjwv)
  recommends indexing policy columns and avoiding per-row authorization-function
  work. D8's exact public lookup uses a B-tree-compatible Site × locale ×
  canonical-path key; staff RLS scope columns and reverse-target monitoring are
  separately indexed and verified at production-shaped volume.
- PostgreSQL's current
  [constraints documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html)
  establishes database-enforced uniqueness and notes the importance of null
  semantics, while its
  [RLS documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html)
  explains that integrity checks bypass row security. D8 makes every namespace
  column non-null, lets the unique constraint decide races, preserves other scope
  through composite foreign keys, and maps integrity failures to authorized,
  non-enumerating domain errors.
- Next.js's current
  [redirect guidance](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/redirecting) documents
  `308` as permanent and method-preserving, so D8 emits it only for `GET`/`HEAD`
  same-Page canonical moves. Its native
  [`notFound`](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/not-found)
  supplies the real `404` plus `noindex` needed for a uniform tombstone without
  introducing a second `410` response owner. Current
  [`revalidateTag`](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag)
  behavior can serve stale-while-revalidate, so cache invalidation remains an
  outbox effect rather than request authorization.
- The live repository reinforces those decisions. The current
  `apps/donor/app/(public)/(solid)/workers/[id]/page.tsx` still generates a mock
  static worker route; the current CMS missionary/project slug indexes are not
  unique; and `apps/donor/lib/cms/client.ts` already distinguishes found,
  not-found, and unavailable results. Phase 22 must replace those legacy route
  assumptions with the exact D8 authority while preserving the useful failure-
  type separation.

## 22. D9 adversarial evidence — release-bound Public Ministry Media Assets

**Status:** Resolved by the founder and ratified as Phase 22 D9 on 2026-08-05.

### 22.1 Scope, conclusion, and ownership boundary

The proposed C-prime direction is correct only after “strip metadata” is made a
verifiable pipeline property rather than an image-library option. Renaming an
upload and deleting EXIF are necessary but insufficient: a source filename can
also be copied into provider display-name fields or embedded XMP/IPTC fields;
location and identity data can survive in maker notes, thumbnails, comments, or
auxiliary images; a valid-looking image can contain active or parser-hostile
content; a private original can become public through a provider default; and a
withdrawn derivative can remain in browser or CDN caches.

The smallest complete Phase 22 boundary is:

- **Phase 22 owns the Public Ministry Media Asset's semantic identity, permitted
  still-image use, placement, candidate/release binding, current public
  eligibility, public derivative requirements, and withdrawal intent.**
- **Phase 29-compatible byte custody owns private original/derivative bytes,
  byte-level scan and transformation execution, copy inventory, storage-provider
  operations, and disposal evidence.** Phase 22 defines and consumes a narrow
  capability contract now; it must not build a parallel general file manager.
- D3 owns which typed public-page block may place the asset. D4/D5 own the
  tenant's existing page review and release behavior. D2 and Phase 10 remain the
  final public-reach and safety ceiling. A media-specific approval queue or a
  provider “moderation” badge must not become a second publication authority.
- The storage or transformation provider proves only the operation it actually
  performed. It does not prove tenant scope, public suitability, Phase 10
  eligibility, page release, cache withdrawal, or that the depicted people
  authorized publication.

This is not optional polish for restricted missionaries. Phase 10 already
requires media geodata scrubbing at the publication firewall. D9 must make the
same safe construction the ordinary path for every public ministry image so a
staff member cannot accidentally select the unsafe path for the person who most
needs it.

### 22.2 Primary-source security evidence

OWASP's current
[File Upload Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html)
requires defense in depth: allowlist only business-required extensions, distrust
the user-supplied Content-Type, validate file signatures without treating them
as sufficient, generate application-owned filenames, authorize uploaders,
enforce size limits, store files outside the webroot or on a separate host,
protect the upload from CSRF, keep parsing libraries current, scan or sandbox
where available, and rewrite images before use. It also names parser exploits,
active client content, XML/ZIP bombs, oversized files, overwrite, public-file
disclosure, and public-retrieval denial of service as separate threats. D9
therefore cannot accept a browser MIME check, one magic-byte test, or a
successful provider upload as proof.

The repository directly pins Sharp 0.34.5. Sharp's current
[constructor documentation](https://sharp.pixelplumbing.com/api-constructor/)
documents a 268,402,689-pixel default input ceiling, a five-channel default,
warning-level failure for untrusted input, one-page processing unless animation
is requested, and an unsafe unlimited mode that removes safety features. Its
[output documentation](https://sharp.pixelplumbing.com/api-output/) says normal
output strips metadata and converts to web-friendly sRGB, while keepMetadata and
withMetadata preserve source metadata; its processing timeout is unlimited
unless configured. Those defaults are useful, but not a Phase 22 contract. The
generic pixel ceiling is far above a ministry-page need, configuration can
silently re-enable metadata, and a no-timeout decode still permits resource
exhaustion.

The permanent control is a bounded, complete decode followed by pixel
reconstruction:

1. The server checks an allowlisted extension hint, declared MIME, magic/file
   signature, and decoder result; disagreement rejects the upload.
2. It enforces explicit source-byte, decoded-pixel, width, height, channel,
   frame/page, CPU-time, memory, and output-byte ceilings. It uses strict
   warning failure, never unlimited decode, and performs no archive or document
   decompression.
3. It decodes exactly one permitted still image, applies the recorded
   orientation to pixels, converts the visible result into controlled sRGB, and
   re-encodes only certified JPEG/WebP derivatives (with optional AVIF only
   after its own production certification).
4. It inspects the produced bytes again: expected signature and dimensions,
   exactly one frame, expected color behavior, decodable output, and no EXIF,
   GPS, IPTC, XMP, maker notes, comments, embedded thumbnail, profile carrying
   source identity/location, or original-name field. A successful function
   return is not the certificate.
5. Malware/sandbox disposition, transform version, input digest, derivative
   digest, decoder/encoder version, and the exact verification result become
   private evidence. Parser detail and raw metadata never enter user-facing
   errors, telemetry, or public records.

ExifTool's official
[metadata-removal FAQ](https://exiftool.org/faq.html) warns that metadata
handling is format-specific and that some color-space information may be needed
for a faithful JPEG. That is an important correction to a blunt “remove every
byte that looks like metadata” rule. D9 should preserve visual fidelity by
rendering the decoded pixels into a controlled output color space, not by
copying an arbitrary source profile or source metadata block. Test fixtures must
include GPS, orientation, maker notes, embedded thumbnails, comments,
copyright/attribution fields, and original-filename-bearing XMP/IPTC fields.

### 22.3 Filename privacy is a multi-surface invariant

The user's requirement is stronger than an opaque storage key. The source
filename must never appear in a public object key, provider public ID or display
name, derivative name, URL or query string, Content-Disposition header, CMS
public serializer, HTML/structured/social metadata, alt text default, logs,
analytics, error tracking, cache key, export, or the generated derivative's
embedded metadata.

Cloudinary's current
[upload parameter documentation](https://cloudinary.com/documentation/upload_parameters)
and
[Image Upload API reference](https://cloudinary.com/documentation/image_upload_api_reference)
show why explicit policy is required. Random public IDs and filename-derived
display names are independent options, and discard_original_filename affects
attachment delivery rather than proving that the source name is absent from
every public surface. The provider can also return media metadata, including
EXIF/IPTC/XMP, to the application. D9 must therefore send an opaque immutable
provider ID, decline any source-filename-derived display name, avoid collecting
raw returned metadata, and independently verify the derivative.

The quiet default should retain no original filename after the intake session.
If a proved support, records, or incident-response need requires it, retain only
the minimum private value under Phase 29 access and retention controls; never
make it a title. The uploader may see the locally selected filename while
choosing a file, but the draft/public preview should use “Photo” or an
editor-authored caption. A download, where a product need is proved, uses a
generic generated name such as ministry-photo.jpg.

### 22.4 Storage, tenant isolation, and provider-default traps

Supabase's current
[Storage bucket fundamentals](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/buckets/fundamentals)
state that buckets are private by default and that public-bucket retrieval
bypasses access control for anyone with the URL. Bucket MIME and size
restrictions are useful first gates, not content proof. Its
[Storage access-control guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/security/access-control)
requires explicit RLS and notes that service keys bypass RLS; upsert additionally
needs SELECT and UPDATE privileges. Its
[upload guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/uploads/standard-uploads)
says inferred Content-Type comes from the extension and concurrent overwrite
semantics differ with upsert. D9 consequently requires:

- a private quarantine/intake bucket with no public read and no client-selected
  final path;
- a server-minted opaque, immutable asset/version key; no rename, move, mutable
  overwrite, or upsert;
- structurally complete Tenant, Legal Entity, Page, asset, candidate/release,
  placement, derivative kind, transform version, and provider-object bindings
  in authoritative relational rows and composite constraints;
- least-privilege commands that re-prove those scopes even when a worker uses a
  service credential that bypasses RLS;
- explicit grants, negative anon/authenticated tests, indexed RLS defense in
  depth, no Realtime exposure, and no folder-prefix-only authorization.

Supabase's own
[hierarchical RLS warning](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/troubleshooting/supabase-storage-inefficient-folder-operations-and-hierarchical-rls-challenges-b05a4d)
explains that Storage “folders” are key prefixes rather than an inherited
permission hierarchy. A tenant path segment may improve operations, but it
cannot be the tenant boundary.

The raw upload is a short-lived **Upload Intake**, not the long-lived media
master. It remains private, non-downloadable through ordinary product surfaces,
and non-authoritative while processing can retry. After successful verification,
Phase 22 references an immutable **Sanitized Media Master Version** reconstructed
from decoded pixels; the raw intake is disposed after a bounded quarantine and
retry interval. If a separately proved records hold or incident-response purpose
requires retaining the raw bytes, Phase 29-compatible custody classifies them as
a distinct restricted object with its own access and disposition evidence. That
exception never makes the raw bytes a reusable media master or a public source.

Cloudinary has a parallel trap.
[Cloudinary access-control documentation](https://cloudinary.com/documentation/control_access_to_media)
distinguishes public upload, private original, and authenticated delivery:
private can protect the original while leaving derived assets publicly
addressable unless strict transformations are enforced. Its
[optimization documentation](https://cloudinary.com/documentation/image_optimization)
says transformed images normally discard most metadata but leave the original
unchanged; transformation flags can preserve IPTC or attribution metadata.
Phase 22 therefore permits no unsigned/browser-authored final upload policy, no
raw-original delivery route, no keep-metadata transformation, no arbitrary
on-demand transformation, and no assumption that a provider's “private” label
protects every derivative. Intake is server-authorized; originals are
authenticated/quarantined; only allowlisted eager derivatives can qualify.

Payload's current
[upload documentation](https://payloadcms.com/docs/upload/overview) exposes
several configuration footguns: bulk upload and paste-from-URL capabilities,
crop/focal-point processing, a metadata-preservation option, configurable image
sizes and filename generation, and an oversize behavior that can truncate
unless abort-on-limit is selected. MIME restrictions do not replace decode
proof. Payload's
[Local API documentation](https://payloadcms.com/docs/local-api/access-control)
also states that Local API operations bypass access control by default unless
overrideAccess is disabled with an acting user; and its
[storage-adapter documentation](https://payloadcms.com/docs/upload/storage-adapters)
warns that direct cloud URLs can bypass Payload access. D9 must use a
purpose-specific Public Ministry Media Asset boundary. A generic Payload Media
document, generic file URL, Local API call, or provider response is not
publication authority.

### 22.5 Format policy and difficult inputs

The browser's accept attribute is only a picker hint, not validation, as both
[MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Attributes/accept)
and the
[HTML Standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html) make clear.
The Phase 22 launch capability should be deliberately narrow:

| Input                                                         | Phase 22 policy                                                                                                                                                 | Permanent reason                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| JPEG, PNG, still WebP                                         | Accept only after signature agreement and complete bounded decode; normalize to certified still derivatives                                                     | Covers ordinary phone and design exports without trusting the source container                                             |
| HEIC/HEIF                                                     | Optional input only when the exact production decoder build and representative phone corpus are certified; always normalize and never deliver the source format | Browser portability is not sufficient, and HEIF may contain multiple images or auxiliary content                           |
| AVIF                                                          | Optional input/output only under separate decode/encode, frame, performance, and browser-fallback certification                                                 | Modern and efficient, but not necessary to make launch safe                                                                |
| GIF, animated WebP/AVIF, APNG, Live Photo or multi-image HEIF | Reject with “Choose a still image”; do not silently select a frame                                                                                              | Silent frame loss can publish unintended content and multiplies parser/resource risk                                       |
| SVG                                                           | Reject                                                                                                                                                          | SVG is active XML, not a photo; scripts, external references, entities, animation, and interaction expand the threat model |
| PDF, office files, archives, audio, video                     | Reject from this capability                                                                                                                                     | They belong to different Phase 29-compatible capabilities and parsers                                                      |

The W3C's
[SVG security and processing model](https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG/conform.html)
and
[SVG media-type security considerations](https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG/mimereg.html)
document script, external-resource, animation, interaction, and XML-entity
risks. Next.js likewise declines to optimize SVG by default and its current
[Image documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/components/image)
requires deliberate Content-Disposition/CSP controls if SVG is enabled. There
is no ministry-photo use case that justifies accepting it. Rasterizing arbitrary
SVG is still an additional parser capability; D9 should reject it rather than
pretend rasterization makes unbounded input harmless.

Public responses must carry the correct allowlisted Content-Type and
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; browsers use response media types and may sniff
ambiguous content, as summarized by
[MDN's MIME-type guidance](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/MIME_types).
Next/Image remotePatterns must name the exact controlled resolver/path rather
than broad provider wildcards.

### 22.6 Release identity, caching, and honest withdrawal

Each qualified derivative is immutable and content-addressed or otherwise bound
to one opaque Asset Version and transform version. A page candidate references
that exact version; release re-proves current Phase 10 eligibility and atomically
pins the exact derivative set into the immutable Page Release. Replacing an
image creates a new asset version and release. It never overwrites bytes behind
the old URL, mutates a released row, or relies on provider cache invalidation to
make the old release mean something different.

Cloudinary's upload documentation notes that invalidation can take seconds to
minutes. Supabase's current
[Smart CDN documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/cdn/smart-cdn)
similarly says object update/deletion propagation can take up to about a minute,
that browser caching is separate, and that a signed URL's token expiry is not a
cached-response purge. Signed URLs are access grants, not a revocation
mechanism. “Delete” and “hide immediately everywhere” are therefore not
equivalent claims.

Normal public derivatives may use content-addressed long caching because a new
release gets a new URL. Phase 10 urgent containment must first make the
application origin and release resolver deny the affected binding, then enqueue
targeted provider/CDN deletion or purge, invalidate the exact page/media cache
surfaces, and record independently observed outcomes. High-risk public media
needs a deliberately bounded browser/shared-cache lifetime or an
application-mediated route so exposure has a known upper bound. The UI may say
“Removed from Asym's live page” after origin containment; it must not promise
recall from visitor caches, screenshots, search indexes, archives, or third
parties.

One immutable Media Release Effect Manifest should cover the exact source asset
version, derivative digests, Page Release/placement, public resolver URL,
responsive variants and social-image use, origin denial state, targeted
invalidation/deletion requests, and observed results. External cache state is
evidence, never current publication authority.

### 22.7 Current repository contradictions that must block D9 release

The current repository contains reusable primitives, but none is safe to adopt
as the Phase 22 authority without this boundary:

1. apps/admin/src/cms/public/serialize-published-page.ts intentionally adds
   media.filename to the public payload and comments that the filename is
   “public by construction.” That directly contradicts D9. Public Ministry
   Media serialization must structurally omit it; a test must fail if any
   source filename reaches public JSON, markup, headers, metadata, or URLs.
2. apps/admin/src/cms/collections/media.ts makes media versionless, uses the
   filename as the admin title, permits GIF, and exposes public static bytes.
   It has image sizes but no D9 asset-version/release certificate. D9 needs a
   purpose-specific projection and migration path; casually changing generic
   CMS media could regress Phase 5 content and is not an acceptable shortcut.
3. packages/ui/components/primitives/image-upload.tsx can upload directly to
   Supabase with a user/time-derived path and upsert, obtain a public URL, or
   accept a Cloudinary public URL. The Cloudinary metadata-registration call
   currently carries tenantId as undefined, and a registration failure is not
   the same atomic success boundary as byte upload. This creates orphan,
   cross-scope, overwrite, and provider-URL-as-truth hazards.
4. packages/lib/cloudinary-client.ts performs a signed direct upload but does
   not itself prove authenticated-original delivery, opaque immutable public
   IDs, strict derivative allowlisting, post-encode privacy verification, or
   Phase 22 release binding.
5. current image configuration accepts broad provider hosts, including
   res.cloudinary.com and wildcard Supabase hosts. A hostile or unrelated
   provider URL must not become eligible merely because its hostname passes a
   renderer allowlist. Public ministry pages should render only the exact
   Asym-controlled release resolver.

These are compatibility facts, not a mandate to delete the generic uploader or
rewrite all Phase 5 media in D9. The permanent Phase 22 fix is one server-owned
intake/finalization seam, followed by a measured migration of only media placed
on typed Public Ministry Pages. Existing generic media remains ineligible until
it is privately reprocessed, verified, and bound as a new Public Ministry Media
Asset Version.

### 22.8 Quiet, accessible contributor and staff experience

The safe pipeline can remain simple:

1. **Choose photo.** Before selection, show accepted still formats, a plain
   maximum, and “We remove location, device details, embedded thumbnails, and
   the original filename from the public copy.” The sentence must not claim the
   original is already deleted if retention or quarantine still holds it.
2. **Adjust.** Show the normalized result, not the unsafe source, in desktop,
   mobile, card, and social crops. Focal-point/crop controls have labelled
   keyboard and button alternatives; no task depends on drag, pinch, hover, or
   color alone.
3. **Describe.** Ask whether the image is informative or decorative. Informative
   images require contextual alt text; decorative images use empty alt text.
   Do not seed alt text from the filename. W3C's current
   [Images Tutorial](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/) requires the text
   alternative to communicate the image's purpose and distinguishes informative,
   decorative, functional, textual, and complex images.
4. **Save draft.** The only visible states are Selected locally, Preparing,
   Ready in draft, Needs attention, Waiting for review when the tenant's D4 mode
   requires it, and Live. “Uploaded” must never imply “public.” A replacement
   leaves the current released photo live until the new derivative is certified
   and a new page release succeeds.

Upload/processing progress and result messages use a restrained live status
region so they are announced without stealing focus, consistent with WCAG 2.2
[status-message guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages).
Errors name the repairable condition in plain language—unsupported format,
animated/multi-image source, corrupt/unreadable file, size/dimension limit, or
processing/scan failure—and identify the affected control, consistent with
[WCAG error-identification guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-identification).
Crop and focal-point actions have single-pointer alternatives under
[WCAG pointer-gesture guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/pointer-gestures).

Healthy assets disappear into the ordinary page editor. Staff see only
actionable exceptions attached to the existing D4/D5 release review: unsafe
format, failed processing, missing alt decision, changed Phase 10 reach,
unresolved represented-person concern, or withdrawal. Technical scan logs and
metadata inventories never become staff chores. Bulk upload, paste-from-URL,
arbitrary provider URL, and “publish anyway” are absent from this capability.

### 22.9 Certification and adversarial test matrix

D9 is not production-authorized until the exact deployed pipeline passes:

- benign JPEG, PNG, still WebP, rotated phone photos, wide-gamut sources, large
  panoramas, zero-byte/truncated/corrupt files, polyglots, spoofed extension and
  MIME, decompression/pixel bombs, excessive channels/dimensions, malformed
  profiles, animation, multi-page/multi-image inputs, and every optionally
  enabled HEIC/AVIF case;
- fixtures carrying GPS, camera/device/owner identity, timestamps, maker notes,
  comments, IPTC/XMP, embedded thumbnails, original filename, preserved filename,
  and alternate/auxiliary imagery, with byte-level output assertions;
- tenant/Legal-Entity/Page/asset/placement scope swaps at every read and write
  boundary; anonymous/authenticated/service-role negative tests; candidate
  supersession, simultaneous finalize, retry, worker crash, stale job,
  provider-success/database-failure, and database-success/provider-timeout;
- immutable URL and digest proof, no overwrite, exact release pinning, old-live-
  until-new-release behavior, D2/Phase 10 narrowing, page retirement, targeted
  cache invalidation, origin denial during provider outage, and honest
  browser/CDN convergence;
- public-response crawling that fails on source filename, raw provider ID,
  private object path, metadata, unauthorized variant, broad remote URL, and
  misleading “live” state;
- keyboard-only upload/crop/remove/retry, screen-reader status and error
  announcements, visible focus, touch targets, zoom/reflow, high contrast,
  reduced motion, and phone network interruption/recovery; and
- production-shaped concurrency, worker fairness, time/memory ceilings,
  quarantine age, transform latency, failure rate, orphan-object detection,
  missing-release derivative detection, and audit-safe alert redaction.

The certification corpus and expected digests/configuration are versioned.
Changing decoder/encoder/library/provider mode, thresholds, output format,
metadata behavior, transform recipe, storage class, public resolver, or cache
policy invalidates the affected certificate and requires a prospective
generation. It never rewrites already released evidence.

### 22.10 Required C-prime-R hardening and binding wording

**Ratified formulation:**

> **C-prime-amended-and-hardened (C-prime-R) — one release-bound,
> Phase-29-compatible Public Ministry Media Asset contract separating
> short-lived private, non-authoritative Upload Intakes from immutable
> Sanitized Media Master Versions and bounded placement-specific Public Media
> Derivative Manifests; with one server-minted single-object Upload Intent,
> opaque application-owned immutable identities, and exact Tenant, Legal
> Entity, Site, subject or purpose, Page, Page Family, locale, placement,
> actor, safety/consent, environment, and processor-generation scope. Every
> qualifying still image passes an allowlist; declared-type, extension-hint,
> signature, and decoder agreement; sandboxed complete bounded one-frame
> decode; malware/sandbox disposition; orientation application; controlled
> sRGB pixel reconstruction; complete re-encoding; and an independent
> post-encode reparse proving exact type, dimensions, digest, frame count, and
> absence of source-derived EXIF, GPS, IPTC, XMP, maker notes, comments,
> embedded thumbnails, auxiliary images, sensitive source profiles, and
> original-name data. The raw intake expires after a bounded retry/quarantine
> interval, and the source filename is discarded after local selection by
> default; any separately proved private retention exception is
> Phase-29-governed and never public. No source filename may enter a durable
> identity,
> storage key, provider ID/display name, delivery URL/query/header, public
> serializer/API/HTML, Open Graph, JSON-LD, sitemap, alt-text default, log,
> analytic, error, export, or generated derivative. Each context-owned Public
> Ministry Media Placement Version pins one semantic role, focal point/crop,
> contextual alt-or-explicit-decorative decision, caption/attribution, exact
> master and derivative manifest, and responsive/card/social variants; D3 owns
> the typed placement, D4/D5 own the sole tenant-selected review/release lane,
> and an immutable Page Release Manifest atomically pins only certified
> derivatives after fresh D2 and Phase 10 reproof. Replacement preserves the
> coherent old live release until the new release succeeds; scope-safe reuse
> has exact where-used evidence; remove-from-this-page is a normal draft;
> urgent remove-everywhere is smallest-scope Phase 10 containment. One
> Asym-controlled opaque resolver rechecks current release and safety before
> selecting private-origin bytes, serves correct typed no-sniff responsive
> output, and records targeted purge/provider outcomes without claiming recall
> from caches, screenshots, downloads, archives, or third parties. Phase 22
> owns public-media meaning, placement, release eligibility, and withdrawal
> intent; Phase-29-compatible custody owns bytes, scans, transforms, copy
> inventory, access, retention, and disposal evidence; providers prove only
> exact operations. Contributors receive one accessible
> choose-check-focus-describe-save flow with honest processing states, while
> healthy media creates
> no second staff queue—without public originals, raw provider URLs, mutable
> overwrite/upsert, MIME/client/provider-default trust, unbounded decode,
> arbitrary transforms or remote fetches, SVG, animation or silent frame
> selection, cross-tenant deduplication, generic Payload Media authority,
> filename-derived title or alt text, AI safety authority, duplicate
> publication authority, or any claim that selected, uploaded, scanned,
> transformed, ready, reviewed, released, cached, withdrawn, deleted, or
> externally forgotten are the same fact.**

This amendment is stricter than the initial option where security is
irreversible and simpler where users work: one still-photo capability, one
ordinary page-release path, one normalized preview, no media security knobs,
and no filename or metadata privacy burden placed on missionaries or staff.

The founder ratified this exact C-prime-R formulation as Phase 22 D9 on
2026-08-05. D9 is therefore binding for subsequent Phase 22 grooming and for
the Phase 29 custody handoff; later work may certify additional capabilities
but may not weaken D9's filename, metadata, immutable-release, safety-reproof,
or authority-separation guarantees.

## 23. D10 — Authenticated exact-version Public Ministry Preview

### 23.1 Decision question and evaluated options

The decision was whether an unreleased Public Ministry Page candidate may be
reviewed only by authenticated users, by a shareable preview credential, or by
an exact currently authorized Principal. The founder selected authenticated
users only, then accepted the hardening that authentication identifies a person
but never by itself authorizes the tenant, page, or version.

The considered shapes were:

1. **Authenticated users only.** Quiet and familiar, but unsafe if interpreted
   as “any valid session may read any draft.” Supabase anonymous users can use
   the `authenticated` database role, Payload authentication does not prove a
   D1 assignment or Phase 12 grant, and object identifiers are not authority.
2. **Expiring shareable link or password.** Convenient for outside reviewers,
   but creates bearer authority, weak revocation, accidental forwarding and log
   leakage, and a second permission system.
3. **Authenticated and currently authorized exact-version preview.** Reuse the
   existing Principal/membership/named-grant system; authorize one page and
   exact saved revision or immutable candidate; recheck every request; keep
   public-equivalent rendering private and side-effect-dark. This is the
   hardened winner.

### 23.2 Current official evidence and resulting constraints

- The [OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html)
  requires deny-by-default behavior and permission validation on every request.
  The
  [OWASP IDOR guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)
  says UUIDs and complex identifiers remain only defense in depth; object-level
  access must still be checked every time. A preview URL or opaque candidate id
  therefore cannot be authority.
- [Supabase anonymous sign-in](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-anonymous)
  documents that anonymous users use the `authenticated` Postgres role and must
  be distinguished by JWT claims. The
  [Supabase RLS guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)
  supports database enforcement, but D10 still needs the Phase 12 product
  decision point because RLS cannot infer page purpose, candidate semantics, or
  inert effects.
- [Payload Local API access control](https://payloadcms.com/docs/local-api/access-control)
  documents that Local API operations bypass access by default unless an acting
  user and `overrideAccess: false` are supplied. Its
  [draft documentation](https://payloadcms.com/docs/versions/drafts) also says
  `draft: true` reads the latest version. Thus `overrideAccess: false` is
  necessary but not sufficient, and a generic draft read contradicts exact-
  version preview.
- [Next.js Draft Mode](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/draft-mode)
  sets a bypass cookie and changes rendering behavior. It does not define
  application authorization, version pinning, or side-effect policy. D10 treats
  it only as rendering plumbing.
- [OWASP session guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html)
  separates authentication, session management, and access control. D10 binds
  the current session to a fresh exact authorization decision rather than
  treating session possession as document access.
- [Google's private-content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/control-what-you-share)
  warns that `noindex` alone does not make content confidential; authorization
  is the actual barrier. D10 therefore combines authenticated authorization
  with `private, no-store`, `noindex`, referrer suppression, and omission from
  discovery rather than advertising SEO controls as security.
- [WCAG 2.2 Accessible Authentication](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/accessible-authentication-minimum)
  requires a path that does not depend on unsupported memory or transcription,
  and recognizes password-manager/autofill and paste support. The preview login
  continuation cannot introduce a copy-a-code or memory-only gate.
- [Vercel preview sharing](https://vercel.com/docs/deployments/sharing-deployments)
  distinguishes individually invited collaborators from anyone-with-link
  access and supports individual revocation. This is useful comparator evidence
  for named access, but D10 deliberately reuses Phase 12 rather than adopting a
  deployment-level share-link permission model.
- Blackbaud's authenticated Participant Center is relevant product precedent
  for authenticated participant workspaces, but it does not prove Asym's exact
  page/version authorization. Comparable product login is UX evidence, not a
  security contract.

### 23.3 Current repository contradictions that block D10 certification

The repository has preview-related primitives, but the current paths are
interim and must not be declared compliant:

1. `apps/admin/app/(payload)/web-studio/preview/[collection]/[id]/page.tsx`
   calls `payload.auth` and uses Payload collection access, but it does not
   prove the D1 assignment or exact Phase 12 page/version capability.
2. The same route calls `findByID` with `draft: true`, which Payload defines as
   the latest draft read, rather than selecting one immutable saved revision or
   submitted candidate.
3. It implements a separate preview renderer with active links. That can drift
   from the donor-facing renderer and trigger navigation or other effects.
4. `readPreviewMedia` accepts `cardURL`, `thumbnailURL`, and raw `url` fields,
   bypassing D9's opaque exact-media resolver and current withdrawal proof.
5. `apps/missionary/app/profile/profile-preview.tsx` mounts functional
   `QuickGive` controls with a preview worker id. A representative preview must
   make all such actions inert by construction.
6. `apps/admin/src/cms-ui/web-studio/collections/config.ts` labels several
   collections `public-link`, a name that conflates released public navigation
   with authenticated unreleased preview.
7. `tests/e2e/cms-publish-flow.spec.ts` proves an unauthenticated redirect but
   not the actor matrix, exact-version stability, current revocation, renderer
   parity, inert effects, response privacy, or D9 media isolation.

These are implementation acceptance gaps, not authorization to change runtime
code during grooming.

### 23.4 Ruthless adversarial matrix

Every requested category has a concern. Likelihood describes realistic product
operation, not an acceptable residual risk.

| Category                          | Concern | What could go wrong and why it matters                                                                                                                                                                                          | Severity | Likelihood | Permanent prevention                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Brittleness                       | **Yes** | A preview assumes “signed in,” `draft: true`, or URL possession is enough; adding a new locale, contributor type, media rendition, or renderer block silently widens access or breaks parity.                                   | Critical | Likely     | One versioned preview contract with exact scope, closed actor/capability registry, explicit unknown-generation failure, production renderer reuse, and contract/property tests for every new page/block/media family.                                                       |
| Technical debt                    | **Yes** | Staff, missionary, review-link, CMS, and live-preview paths develop separate authentication, rendering, banners, and effect suppression; every bug must be fixed repeatedly.                                                    | High     | Likely     | One Phase 5 preview adapter over the public reader/renderer and one Phase 12 decision point; small actor adapters select the exact version but do not fork semantics. Remove the interim renderer only after parity proof.                                                  |
| Edge cases                        | **Yes** | A spouse loses access while a tab is open; the tenant switches; a reviewer expires; a new save occurs; a locale/media version disappears; a page becomes unsafe; a session expires mid-preview.                                 | Critical | Likely     | Reauthorize every HTML/data/media/refresh request; pin exact version; show deliberate newer-version action; same-origin login continuation; Phase 10/D9 narrowing wins next fetch; fail closed on missing generation.                                                       |
| Footguns                          | **Yes** | A staff member copies a preview URL, a developer treats Draft Mode or `authenticated` as authority, a contributor clicks an active Give/form control, or a service role bypasses the intended path.                             | Critical | Likely     | No Share action or bearer endpoint; capability lint and route architecture test; side-effect-dark renderer mode; service execution must carry verified EffectiveAccess; explicit Preview-not-public banner.                                                                 |
| Tenant safety                     | **Yes** | Changing an opaque page/version id exposes another Tenant, Legal Entity, Site, page, contributor, locale, or candidate; cached preview content crosses sessions.                                                                | Critical | Possible   | Repeat exact scope on authoritative rows and lookups; composite same-scope keys; Phase 12 PDP plus forced RLS defense in depth; `private, no-store`; cross-scope substitution tests including anonymous-Supabase users.                                                     |
| Over-engineering                  | **Yes** | A new guest directory, invitation product, token vault, password layer, comment system, reviewer role matrix, or per-block preview ACL duplicates Phase 12 and confuses tenants.                                                | High     | Likely     | Existing verified Principal plus one `public_pages.preview` named grant; one Preview action; no comments or new workflow in D10; D4/D5 remain sole review authority.                                                                                                        |
| UX/UI and user friction           | **Yes** | Users cannot tell draft from live, which version they see, why controls do nothing, or how to recover after login; auth challenges exclude users with cognitive or motor disabilities.                                          | High     | Likely     | Persistent exact-version banner, separate View live page, explicit inert-control copy, responsive presets, clear unavailable/newer-version states, focus/status announcements, password-manager/paste/autofill support, accessible authentication testing.                  |
| Hidden coupling                   | **Yes** | Preview is mistaken for review approval, Phase 10 consent, D9 processing, D2 public reach, D7 Giving readiness, notification dispatch, analytics, or publication.                                                               | Critical | Likely     | Separate owner facts and commands; preview manifest references but never recreates them; no state transition on view; effect-free renderer contract; terminology tests prohibit “approved/live” inference.                                                                  |
| Failure modes                     | **Yes** | Auth, authorization, Payload versions, renderer registry, media resolver, or owner data times out and the route falls back to latest/live/raw content or reports not found.                                                     | Critical | Possible   | Fail closed to one non-enumerating no-store unavailable envelope; private cause code; no fallback; bounded retry only for safe reads; prior live page remains independently available through its own route.                                                                |
| Data integrity risks              | **Yes** | Reviewer sees revision A but approval applies to B; mutable latest changes during inspection; locale/profile/media generations do not match; stale grant remains cached.                                                        | Critical | Likely     | Immutable revision/candidate digest and exact compatibility pins; approval references same candidate; monotonic authorization epoch; no shared preview cache; CAS/current proof before any later release command.                                                           |
| Security and privacy risks        | **Yes** | IDOR, token leakage, browser/history/referrer/cache leakage, XSS, unsafe media URLs, existence or timing oracles, or service-role bypass exposes a restricted missionary.                                                       | Critical | Possible   | Object-level authorization every request; no bearer credentials; private/no-store/referrer suppression; closed sanitized renderer; D9 resolver; uniform unavailable response; telemetry redaction; CSP and automated attack matrix.                                         |
| Scalability and performance risks | **Yes** | Per-request proof becomes N+1, full rendering saturates shared tenants, or media checks make preview unusable; teams work around it with screenshots or public drafts.                                                          | High     | Possible   | One indexed set-based authorization query, batched projection/media manifest reads, bounded render/cardinality contracts, tenant-fair limits, measured latency SLO, and no authorization caching beyond the current epoch-safe request.                                     |
| Operational burden                | **Yes** | Staff repeatedly invite people, manage bespoke passwords/tokens, explain stale views, manually disable effects, or require developers to diagnose every denied preview.                                                         | High     | Likely     | Reuse ordinary onboarding and named grants; default contributor/reviewer access is automatic from existing authority; one cause-coded exception/explainer; automatic expiry/revocation; no routine preview administration.                                                  |
| Observability gaps                | **Yes** | Teams cannot distinguish authentication failure, wrong active tenant, revoked grant, stale epoch, missing revision, incompatible renderer, D9 withdrawal, or a blocked effect without logging sensitive content.                | High     | Likely     | Privacy-safe correlation id and reason taxonomy; metrics for denied/cross-scope/stale/outage/inert-effect attempts; protected `explainAccess`; no content, filename, legal identity, URL credential, or bearer secret in logs.                                              |
| Dependency and integration risks  | **Yes** | Payload changes latest-draft/version semantics, Next changes Draft Mode, Supabase anonymous sessions pass `authenticated`, a media/CDN URL bypasses D9, or deployment protection is mistaken for product access.                | Critical | Possible   | Version-pinned adapters and conformance tests; Phase 12 authorization independent of framework roles/cookies; exact Payload version reads; D9 opaque delivery only; dependency changes recertify the affected generation.                                                   |
| Migration and upgrade risks       | **Yes** | Existing `/preview/:collection/:id` links and `public-link` config are grandfathered, bookmarks keep mutable behavior, or cutover leaves two preview authorities.                                                               | Critical | Likely     | Complete route/config/link census; shadow parity and actor tests; one cutover to the D10 adapter; old endpoints become non-authoritative or removed; no redirect that converts a legacy id into access; append-only evidence of migration exceptions.                       |
| Other development hazards         | **Yes** | TOCTOU between authorization and version/media reads, revocation races, client hydration re-enables controls, prefetch invokes an action, test-mode auth bypass leaks into production, or partial deployment mixes generations. | Critical | Possible   | Recheck/consume exact scope inside one server boundary; signed compatible generation manifest; server-enforced inertness, not disabled UI alone; no mutating GET/prefetch; non-prod auth guardrails; concurrency, property, hydration, deployment-skew, and rollback tests. |

### 23.5 Ruthless synthesis and implementation order

1. **Close the bearer seam first.** Remove Phase 5's reserved shareable-token
   authority from every normative contract. Preserve D2's already released
   **Shared by link — public** reach as a separate anonymous state.
2. **Define one exact target.** A working-preview target is a coherently saved
   immutable Page Revision; a review-preview target is the exact D4 candidate.
   Never use mutable `latest` as the contract.
3. **Reuse Phase 12.** Add the distinct `public_pages.preview` atom and map D1
   contributors, staff reviewers, and optional named grantees through the same
   PDP, current assignment, floor, epoch, expiry, and revocation path.
4. **Converge the renderer.** Route exact authorized content through Phase 5's
   production-equivalent renderer and D9 resolver with server-enforced inert
   effects. The current admin renderer remains explicitly interim until parity
   and migration proof are complete.
5. **Make privacy and failure structural.** Apply private/no-store/noindex/
   referrer-suppressed output, uniform unavailable responses, no fallback, and
   exact request-time safety/media reproof to every dependent request.
6. **Ship the quiet experience.** One Preview action, one persistent exact-
   version banner, deliberate newer-version selection, separate live-page link,
   responsive presets, accessible auth/controls/status, and no share surface.
7. **Certify before cutover.** Run the complete actor, scope, revocation,
   exact-version, renderer, effect, media, header/crawler, accessibility,
   outage, concurrency, and deployment-skew matrix against production-shaped
   data. Cut over once; do not operate legacy and D10 authority in parallel.

This order is both safer and simpler than bolting authorization onto an
existing mutable preview after the fact. It also gives contributors and staff
the fewest reasonable steps: save, select Preview, inspect the exact result,
return to edit or review.

### 23.6 Required A-prime-R wording

> **A-prime-amended-and-hardened (A-prime-R) — one
> authenticated-and-currently-authorized, exact-version Public Ministry
> Preview with no bearer preview access.**

The founder ratified this exact formulation as Phase 22 D10 on 2026-08-06.
D10 closes Phase 5's reserved shareable non-staff preview-token seam. Earlier
research about preview tokens remains historical comparator evidence and grants
no implementation authority. D1 contributor assignments, D2 **Shared by link —
public** reach, D4/D5 review/release, D9 media safety, Phase 10 ceilings, and
Phase 12 authorization remain intact and independently authoritative.

## 24. D11 Epistle primary-source research — updates, feeds, email, and audience truth

This subsection records the primary-source evidence requested for D11. It does
not choose Asym product policy. It distinguishes what Epistle documents, what
was observed on one live Epistle site, what Epistle merely markets, and what no
public source establishes. Sources were accessed on **2026-08-06** unless an
article date is stated. Epistle pages generally do not publish revision dates;
the XML sitemap's `lastmod` value is useful freshness evidence but is not proof
that every sentence on the page was reviewed on that date.
