   reordered, timeout-after-commit, concurrent-tab, stale-version, and offline
   replay conditions;
5. replies cannot cross post/space or exceed one level, and hide/redact/remove
   preserves or tombstones descendants deterministically;
6. author, contributor, missionary, staff moderator, commenter, reporter,
   restricted actor, and blocked actor permissions match the exact source and
   tenant scope;
7. HTML/script, malformed Unicode, unsafe links, oversized input, spam bursts,
   report abuse, and expensive pagination remain bounded;
8. profile/avatar substitution and export/erasure/retention paths do not leak
   raw PII or break audit integrity;
9. notification occurrence generation dedupes and respects mute/preferences
   without claiming dispatch or delivery; and
10. keyboard-only, screen-reader, 320 CSS-pixel reflow, zoom, target size,
    status announcement, focus recovery, reduced-motion, mobile latency, and
    degraded-network behavior meet the documented interaction contract.

### 26.9 Founder choice subsequently ratified

The recommended next choice is **Option C-prime — Bounded Supporter Response
Profiles**. It is the smallest option that preserves Epistle's meaningful
supporter-response loop while letting a tenant choose no interaction or
acknowledgements only when it lacks the need, safety posture, or moderation
capacity for comments.

This research section did not itself create authority. The founder subsequently
ratified the hardened C-prime-R in §27 as Phase 22 D12 on 2026-08-06; the
durable architectural record is
[ADR-0129](../../adr/0129-bounded-supporter-response-profiles.md).

## 27. Ratified D12 adversarial review — bounded Supporter Response Profiles

**Status:** Ratified and adversarially hardened on 2026-08-06.

**Reviewed:** 2026-08-06

**Question:** whether one tenant profile choosing **Responses off**, **Like + I
prayed**, or **Like + I prayed + comments** can deliver the Epistle-style
connection loop without creating a public social network, unsafe audience
leakage, hidden moderation work, misleading UI, or an unmaintainable policy
engine.

### 27.1 Verdict

**C-prime is directionally correct, but the short formulation is not safe or
implementation-ready on its own.** Every adversarial category has a real
concern. The permanent answer is a hardened C-prime-R with:

- **Responses off as the safe initial default**, followed by one guided,
  prospective tenant choice. Choosing comments reveals only the minimum
  additional moderation controls needed to operate comments safely.
- an immutable **Supporter Response Profile Version** that acts as a ceiling;
  an update may inherit it or narrow it, never broaden it;
- one exact, audience-bound **Engagement Space** per D11 Supporter Release
  Projection, with current authorization re-proved on every operation;
- public releases that remain read-only and reveal no supporter response
  identities, bodies, counts, cursors, moderation states, or realtime events;
- two code-owned acknowledgement types, **Like** and **I prayed**, plus an
  optional bounded comment thread. There is no tenant reaction builder;
- reversible, evidence-preserving moderation and a quiet exception queue,
  rather than destructive staff edits or a mandatory review treadmill;
- honest committed-state UX, idempotent writes, audience-scoped counts,
  bounded input and pagination, privacy-safe identity projection, and
  preference-aware notification occurrences; and
- an explicit migration boundary that does not reinterpret the existing demo
  `love`/`prayer`/`fire` counters and comments as certified D12 truth.

This is necessary complexity caused by private supporter conversation. It is
not permission to add arbitrary reactions, deep threads, media comments,
mentions, direct messages, public replies, gamification, or a social graph.

### 27.2 What current primary sources establish

The following are **documented product or standards facts**, not claims that
another product's whole design is appropriate for Asym:

- **Epistle:** its current first-party tour says ministry partners can respond
  with likes, prayers, comments, and giving; missionaries receive insight into
  opens, likes, prayers, and comments; and recipients choose daily, weekly, or
  monthly email grouping. Its security page documents ministry-partner-only
  private posts, an invisible site mode requiring login, and secure
  notification emails that omit update content; it also warns that the product
  does not replace an organization's security strategy for high-risk contexts.
  This validates the low-friction acknowledgement loop, batched communication,
  and safety ceiling. Epistle's public pages do **not** document the exact
  comment audience, moderation states, reporting, blocking, retention,
  deletion, RLS, or notification-failure semantics, so none of those may be
  inferred from the marketing copy. Sources: [Epistle
  tour](https://www.epistle.org/tour/), [Epistle security](https://www.epistle.org/security/).
- **Ghost:** native comments are restricted to logged-in members; access can be
  limited to all members or paid members; and its theme helper shows comments
  only when comments are enabled and the reader can access the post. Members
  can create, edit, delete, reply, react to, and report comments. Staff can
  search/filter moderation views and reversibly hide/show comments. Authors,
  repliers, and owners receive different comment notifications, with at least
  reply notifications configurable by the member. This supports authenticated
  audience scoping, contextual moderation, reversible visibility, and
  recipient-owned preferences. Sources: [Ghost comments](https://ghost.org/help/commenting/),
  [Ghost comments helper](https://docs.ghost.org/themes/helpers/data/comments).
- **Patreon:** current first-party documentation exposes per-post comment
  access, remembers a creator's default for future posts, leaves existing posts
  unchanged, keeps earlier comments visible to the creator when comments are
  disabled, rate-limits some writers, and makes auto-moderated comments visible
  only to the creator and commenter with a restore action. Its default of
  allowing anyone on new public posts and its optional media comments are
  explicitly **not** safe defaults for Phase 22. Source: [Patreon comment
  settings](https://support.patreon.com/hc/en-us/articles/19789361628045-Comment-settings).
- **Substack:** reader reports enter a review surface with approve/remove
  outcomes and a daily report email. Its newer Reply Rules hide rather than
  immediately delete suspected violations and allow later restoration. The
  documented exclusion of some paid, followed, or contributor accounts from
  automatic rules is an anti-pattern for Asym: trusted or donating actors must
  not bypass baseline abuse controls. Sources: [Substack comment
  moderation](https://support.substack.com/hc/en-us/articles/5780832770452-Can-I-moderate-comments-on-my-Substack-posts),
  [Substack Reply Rules](https://support.substack.com/hc/en-us/articles/49712271829012-What-are-Reply-Rules-on-Substack).
- **GoFundMe:** current comments require both a signed-in account and a prior
  donation, support replies, and allow the commenter to delete their own
  comment. This is evidence for relationship-gated writing, not justification
  to use a payment row as Asym's authorization source; Asym's purpose-authorized
  supporter relationship can arise from multiple source systems and must be
  re-proved independently. Source: [GoFundMe comments and words of
  support](https://support.gofundme.com/hc/en-us/articles/204191158-Adding-and-editing-words-of-support-or-comments).
- **Givebutter:** campaign pages can expose a public supporter feed containing
  donation identity, amount, messages, and comments; turning off public
  messages can still expose a billing name unless the donor chose anonymity;
  hiding a post removes the whole transaction presentation and requires vendor
  support to restore it; and donor comment emails are documented as not
  configurable. These are useful counterexamples: engagement must not be
  coupled to donation presentation, moderation must be reversible by an
  authorized tenant, and response notifications must be preference-aware.
  Sources: [Givebutter supporter-feed visibility](https://help.givebutter.com/en/articles/3586667-how-to-hide-messages-in-the-supporter-feed),
  [Givebutter campaign notifications](https://help.givebutter.com/en/articles/6552003-how-to-set-campaign-notifications).
- **W3C:** WCAG 2.2 requires programmatically determinable control state and
  status messages, descriptive text for detected errors, visible focus,
  keyboard operation, reflow, and at least a 24-by-24 CSS-pixel target or the
  defined spacing exception. The ARIA button pattern uses `aria-pressed` for a
  stable-label toggle and Enter/Space activation. APG examples are informative
  and explicitly require real assistive-technology testing before production.
  Sources: [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), [status
  messages](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html),
  [target size](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html),
  [button pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/button/).
- **OWASP:** authorization should use least privilege, deny by default, and
  validate permissions on every request; relationship/attribute checks are
  preferable to coarse roles for object access. Untrusted strings require
  context-correct output encoding, and untrusted URLs require protocol
  validation. APIs need explicit body, list, operation, rate, and cost bounds.
  Security logs must be protected and must not casually retain tokens,
  sensitive personal data, or full private content. Sources: [OWASP
  Authorization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html),
  [XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html),
  [API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa4-unrestricted-resource-consumption/),
  [Logging Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html).
- **Supabase and PostgreSQL:** RLS is appropriate for row-level tenant and
  relationship enforcement, but Supabase service credentials and Postgres
  `BYPASSRLS` roles bypass policies. PostgreSQL table owners normally bypass
  RLS unless `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` is used, and referential-integrity
  checks can create covert information channels. Supabase recommends indexes
  on policy columns and documents policy-query patterns that avoid repeated
  per-row function work. RLS is therefore one required layer, not proof that
  an elevated command, cache, count, stream, or constraint cannot leak data.
  Sources: [Supabase RLS](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security),
  [PostgreSQL current row-security policies](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html).

The design conclusions below are **Asym inferences** from those facts, the
eleven Phase 22 decisions that preceded D12,
the current-worktree audit in section 26, and the named Phase boundaries. They
are not advertised guarantees of the comparison products.

### 27.3 Hardened UX contract

#### Tenant setup

The tenant sees one setting at **Ministry updates → Supporter responses**:

1. **Responses off — safest default.** “Supporters can read updates but cannot
   respond in Asym.”
2. **Like + I prayed.** “Supporters can acknowledge an update. No comments or
   moderation inbox.”
3. **Like + I prayed + comments.** “Supporters can acknowledge and discuss an
   update. Your team can hide or review reported comments.”

Use three radio cards, not three independent switches. Each card shows a
compact supporter preview, who can see the responses, and the expected staff
work. Selecting comments progressively reveals only:

- **When comments appear:** **Right away, with reporting** or **After review**;
- **Who handles exceptions:** one existing tenant role/permission group, not a
  new user list; and
- an editable community-guidelines link or short tenant statement.

The review page states the exact effective boundary and consequences:
“Applies to Ministry Updates released after 1 September 2026. Existing updates
do not change.” A separate, explicit **Manage existing responses** action may
create bounded close/reopen occurrences after showing the affected update
count; a profile edit never silently retrofits old releases. A distinct
permissioned **Pause new responses** safety action can immediately narrow an
affected tenant/source scope without destroying prior conversation.

#### Missionary and contributor experience

- The update composer shows one quiet inherited summary, for example
  **Supporters can like, say they prayed, and comment**. A secondary control may
  narrow that update to acknowledgements only or responses off. It cannot
  broaden beyond the tenant ceiling.
- After release, the author sees a compact summary and unread-comment count.
  Individual responders and comment bodies remain behind progressive
  disclosure; healthy activity does not create an operations queue.
- An exact D1-authorized contributor may hide an unsafe comment and close new
  comments on that source. Tenant moderation staff own restore, redact, and
  actor-restriction outcomes. Neither role can rewrite a supporter's words.
- A correction or superseding Update Revision clearly says when a response was
  made against an earlier revision. Conversation does not silently move to
  text the supporter never saw.

#### Supporter experience

- Public pages remain read-only. When a protected Supporter projection exists,
  a quiet **Supporter? Sign in to respond** link may open that projection after
  authorization. The public response area never renders protected counts or a
  tantalizing “private comments exist” state.
- **Like** and **I prayed** are stable-label native toggle buttons with visible
  selected states and `aria-pressed`. Counts are secondary. The action remains
  reversible because duplicate taps, changed intent, and accidental input are
  realistic; append-only occurrences preserve the evidence.
- If comments are enabled, the composer says **Visible to supporters who can
  read this update** and previews the exact display name/avatar others will
  see. Text survives sign-in expiry, network loss, authorization change, and a
  rejected submission until the user discards it.
- The UI distinguishes **Sending**, **Posted**, **Waiting for review**, **Not
  posted — retry**, and **Comments closed**. A timeout or local optimistic row
  is never styled as durable success without committed readback.
- Comments use bounded plain text, sanitized `http`/`https` links with safe
  link attributes, keyset pagination, and at most one reply level. Phase 22 has
  no media comments, rich HTML, embeds, polls, mentions, arbitrary emoji,
  private messages, or infinite feed.
- Users can edit their own comment through immutable revisions, withdraw its
  presentation, report another comment, and mute that conversation. A neutral
  tombstone remains only when needed to preserve a visible reply.

#### Moderation and notifications

- **Right away, with reporting** is the low-friction default after a tenant
  affirmatively enables comments for an authenticated supporter audience.
  **After review** is available for restricted or higher-risk tenants, but is
  not forced on every tenant.
- Every visible comment has **Report** with a short code-owned reason list and
  optional detail. Duplicate reports coalesce. Reported, held, or
  contributor-hidden content alone enters the exception-first staff queue.
- Hide/restore is the ordinary reversible action. Privacy/safety redaction and
  retention deletion are explicit append-only outcomes with actor, reason,
  prior revision, scope, and time. A block/restriction applies at the smallest
  authorized relationship/source scope and is re-proved before the next read
  or write.
- No supporter class, donor amount, staff role, contributor relationship, or
  “trusted” badge bypasses size, rate, link, duplicate, malware/XSS, reporting,
  or audit controls. Automated classification may hold an item, but is
  non-authoritative, explainable to staff, reversible, and never the only
  safety layer.
- Phase 22 emits typed, deduplicable response occurrences. Phases 17/6 own
  channel, consent, cadence, mute, batching, dispatch, and provider outcome.
  Default author email is a digest, not one message per reaction. A direct
  reply may be immediate only when the recipient's preference allows it.

### 27.4 Ruthless category-by-category review

#### 27.4.1 Brittleness — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** a design keyed only by Update ID, current tenant
  default, or login state breaks when one canonical Update has Public and
  Supporter projections, a profile changes, access is revoked, or an Update is
  corrected.
- **Why it matters:** responses can appear under the wrong audience or revision
  and settings can silently change old conversations.
- **Severity:** Critical. **Likelihood:** Likely if the prototype model is
  extended.
- **Permanent prevention:** immutable profile/release versions; a complete
  Engagement Space key; current audience reproof on every operation; explicit
  close/reopen occurrences; and failure tests for stale tabs, revoked access,
  corrections, and same-Update multi-audience projection.

#### 27.4.2 Technical debt — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** legacy `love`/`prayer`/`fire` counters, mutable post
  totals, read-only demo comment writes, and destructive admin comment APIs are
  wrapped instead of replaced.
- **Why it matters:** misleading success states and incompatible storage become
  permanent public contracts.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Likely.
- **Permanent prevention:** introduce one typed engagement boundary and new
  occurrence/projection schema; retire the demo transports; keep reusable UI
  primitives only after they meet D12 semantics; publish a migration manifest
  rather than reinterpreting old rows.

#### 27.4.3 Edge cases — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** session expiry mid-comment, two tabs toggling, mobile
  offline replay, comments closing during submit, a hidden parent with visible
  replies, self-edit after a report, identity-display changes, Unicode/bidi
  abuse, source retirement, or an author losing assignment produces duplicates,
  lost text, dangling replies, or unauthorized reads.
- **Why it matters:** these are normal lifecycle events, not theoretical
  anomalies.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Likely over time.
- **Permanent prevention:** idempotency keys, optimistic concurrency, committed
  readback, preserved drafts, one-level reply constraints, deterministic
  tombstones, immutable display-at-post evidence plus current privacy
  projection, exact lifecycle containment, and a documented state-transition
  test matrix.

#### 27.4.4 Footguns — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** an admin accidentally enables public comments,
  believes a prospective setting changed history, grants broad moderator
  access, edits a supporter's words, or assumes an elevated Supabase command is
  protected by RLS.
- **Why it matters:** one plausible click or helper function could expose
  sensitive ministry conversation or destroy trust.
- **Severity:** Critical. **Likelihood:** Possible–Likely.
- **Permanent prevention:** no public-write option; radio-card modes with
  consequences and preview; future-effective activation; separate explicit
  historical closure; fixed permission bundles; staff hide/redact rather than
  impersonating edits; and authorization inside every elevated command.

#### 27.4.5 Tenant safety — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** comments, counts, identities, cache entries, cursors,
  realtime events, reports, or notifications cross Tenant, Legal Entity,
  environment, purpose, source, audience, or Update Revision.
- **Why it matters:** this is a direct cross-tenant confidentiality incident.
- **Severity:** Critical. **Likelihood:** Possible without structural controls.
- **Permanent prevention:** carry every isolation coordinate structurally;
  same-scope foreign keys/constraints; deny-by-default RLS and application
  authorization; private raw tables; audience-scoped caches and streams; no
  global count; substitution and non-enumeration tests; and service-role usage
  limited to narrow commands after permission proof.

#### 27.4.6 Over-engineering — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** tenant-defined emoji, arbitrary ACL/workflow rules,
  deep replies, media, mentions, DMs, social profiles, ranking, realtime fanout,
  and per-update configuration turn a ministry-update response seam into a
  social network.
- **Why it matters:** complexity raises moderation, safety, accessibility, and
  maintenance costs without improving the core acknowledgement loop.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Likely without a hard boundary.
- **Permanent prevention:** exactly three modes, two acknowledgement types,
  one optional moderation posture, one reply level, plain text, exception-first
  operations, no public writes, and no new microservice or generalized policy
  engine.

#### 27.4.7 UX/UI and user friction — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** independent toggles create invalid combinations;
  icon-only prayer/like controls are ambiguous; hidden audience rules chill
  comments; optimistic failures lie; premoderation surprises writers; endless
  lists and tiny menus fail mobile/accessibility; alerts overwhelm authors and
  staff.
- **Why it matters:** supporters stop responding, missionaries stop posting,
  and staff disable the feature to escape noise.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Likely.
- **Permanent prevention:** three mutually exclusive radio cards with preview;
  progressive disclosure; visible audience/identity copy at compose time;
  labelled 44-by-44-preferred targets meeting at least WCAG 2.5.8; stable toggle
  semantics; preserved input; exact status/error messages; bounded Load more;
  calm summaries; per-recipient mute/digest preferences; and usability tests
  with older adults, keyboard and screen-reader users, missionaries, and small
  tenant teams.

#### 27.4.8 Hidden coupling — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** engagement mutates D11 release truth, donation rows
  become supporter authorization, response totals become CRM relationship
  truth, or notification delivery is inferred from a comment occurrence.
- **Why it matters:** a change in giving, publishing, CRM, or messaging can
  corrupt another domain.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Possible–Likely.
- **Permanent prevention:** D11 owns released content/audience; Phase 9/28 owns
  relationship truth; D12 owns response occurrences/projections; D7/13 owns
  giving; Phases 17/6 own notification delivery; use stable IDs and typed
  events between them with no duplicated authority.

#### 27.4.9 Failure modes — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** timeout after commit duplicates a response; the
  classifier, realtime stream, count projector, or notification provider fails;
  a stale client posts after closure; or a moderation action partially applies.
- **Why it matters:** users see false success, harmful content leaks, or valid
  comments disappear.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Likely across the system lifetime.
- **Permanent prevention:** idempotent commands; inspect-before-retry;
  transactionally committed occurrence plus outbox; CAS/version checks;
  smallest-scope fail-closed writes; last-known safe reads only while still
  authorized; honest degraded UI; resumable projection repair; and atomic
  moderation state transitions.

#### 27.4.10 Data integrity risks — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** duplicate acknowledgements, negative counts,
  orphaned replies, count drift, comment-to-wrong-revision attachment,
  in-place staff edits, or migration of `fire` as a fabricated Like corrupts
  history.
- **Why it matters:** the missionary-facing summary and audit trail disagree.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Likely without occurrence constraints.
- **Permanent prevention:** append-only typed occurrences; one current
  acknowledgement per actor/type/space; deterministic reduction; same-space
  reply constraints; immutable comment revisions; reconciled projections;
  idempotent repair; and legacy rows marked unverified unless their exact scope
  and identity can be proved.

#### 27.4.11 Security and privacy risks — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** IDOR/BOLA, public-cache leakage, XSS/phishing links,
  enumeration through counts or constraints, raw donor-profile joins,
  overbroad moderation access, sensitive comment bodies in logs, or indefinite
  retention exposes missionaries and supporters.
- **Why it matters:** ministry updates can contain location, relationship,
  religious-belief, prayer, and vulnerable-person context.
- **Severity:** Critical. **Likelihood:** Possible–Likely.
- **Permanent prevention:** relationship- and projection-bound authorization on
  every request; public/private cache separation; safe output sinks and URL
  validation; non-enumerating errors; privacy-safe display identities; field-
  and purpose-scoped moderator views; no bodies/PII in ordinary telemetry;
  encryption, export, erasure/redaction, legal hold, and bounded retention owned
  by the applicable privacy phases.

#### 27.4.12 Scalability and performance risks — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** reaction storms, per-row authorization functions,
  recursive reply queries, offset scans, live count updates, and one
  notification per reaction overload the database and staff inboxes.
- **Why it matters:** a popular update should not slow unrelated tenants or
  convert engagement into unbounded provider cost.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Possible, then Likely with growth.
- **Permanent prevention:** indexed policy/scope columns; set-based RLS helper
  patterns; bounded keyset pagination; one reply level; tenant-fair rate and
  concurrency limits; transactional audience-local projections; batched
  response occurrences; backpressure; load tests with skewed high-activity
  tenants; and no public realtime requirement for launch.

#### 27.4.13 Operational burden — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** every comment requires approval, every reaction
  sends email, settings are repeated per page, or staff need vendor support to
  restore content.
- **Why it matters:** small nonprofit teams will abandon the feature or leave
  harmful content unattended.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Likely if comments are treated as a
  generic social feed.
- **Permanent prevention:** Responses off by default; acknowledgement-only mode;
  one inherited tenant profile; right-away-with-reporting as the normal comment
  posture; optional review-first; an exception-only queue; reversible self-
  service moderation; role-group assignment; digest defaults; and workload
  preview before enabling comments.

#### 27.4.14 Observability gaps — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** authorization denials, projection lag, count drift,
  dropped notification occurrences, classifier holds, report backlog, or
  cross-scope attempts remain invisible—or debugging logs leak the comments.
- **Why it matters:** staff cannot tell a quiet healthy tenant from a broken
  response surface, and engineers cannot recover safely.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Likely without deliberate telemetry.
- **Permanent prevention:** privacy-safe metrics and traces keyed by opaque
  scope IDs; authorization-denial and substitution signals; projection
  watermark/drift checks; queue age and failure-class dashboards; audit access
  logs; synthetics for each mode; alerts on leakage invariants; and strict
  exclusion of comment bodies, tokens, email addresses, and raw names.

#### 27.4.15 Dependency and integration risks — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** an AI/spam vendor outage blocks all comments, changes
  classification behavior, retains private text, or a notification provider
  retry duplicates messages.
- **Why it matters:** Asym cannot outsource authorization, privacy, or final
  moderation judgment.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Possible.
- **Permanent prevention:** deterministic local validation and rate limits;
  optional capability-labelled classifiers with tenant-approved data handling;
  hold-and-review degradation when a required classifier is unavailable;
  provider-independent occurrences/outbox; idempotent delivery; kill switches;
  and no third-party script or public comment widget in the protected surface.

#### 27.4.16 Migration and upgrade risks — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** old mutable counters and comments are assigned new
  semantics they never proved; a schema or RLS upgrade temporarily opens rows;
  or a policy-version change rewrites old audience behavior.
- **Why it matters:** migration can create false supporter history or a brief
  but serious privacy breach.
- **Severity:** Critical. **Likelihood:** Possible.
- **Permanent prevention:** source-covered migration manifests; no `fire` →
  Like inference; shadow reconciliation; versioned policies; expand/migrate/
  contract deployment; production-shaped RLS tests before grants; fail-closed
  rollback that preserves occurrences; and portable tenant/self export.

#### 27.4.17 Other development hazards — concern: **yes**

- **What could go wrong:** TOCTOU between authorization and write, count races,
  duplicate retry keys, cache poisoning, report brigading, unrestricted search,
  unsafe moderation bulk actions, weak test fixtures, or unclear product/on-call
  ownership creates harm outside the main happy path.
- **Why it matters:** concurrency and abuse failures often appear only in
  production and are hard to reverse after notification or public exposure.
- **Severity:** High. **Likelihood:** Possible–Likely.
- **Permanent prevention:** authorize and mutate in one database command where
  possible; bind idempotency to actor/action/space/body hash; use CAS and unique
  constraints; bound search and bulk actions; coalesce abusive reports;
  adversarial multi-tenant/concurrency/fuzz/accessibility tests; staged release
  with per-mode kill switches; named product/security/operations owners; and a
  rehearsed containment and recovery runbook.

### 27.5 Ruthless synthesis — the best permanent path

Implement D12 in this order; later steps must not be used to compensate for a
missing earlier guarantee:

1. **Freeze the bounded product contract.** Three modes only; initial default
   off; two fixed acknowledgements; optional comments; public read-only;
   per-update narrowing only; no new social features.
2. **Establish authority before UI.** Define versioned Response Profiles,
   exact Engagement Spaces, display-identity projections, current audience
   authorization, same-scope constraints, retention/custody references, and
   phase-owned typed events.
3. **Replace prototype truth.** Introduce append-only acknowledgement and
   comment-revision occurrences, moderation outcomes, idempotent commands, and
   reconciled audience-local projections. Quarantine legacy rows that lack
   exact proof; do not adapt the demo no-op write into production.
4. **Ship the acknowledgement-only vertical slice first.** Certify cross-scope
   denial, revocation, concurrency, counts, caching, accessibility, responsive
   behavior, and quiet author summaries using the same final Engagement Space
   seam.
5. **Add comments as an optional capability.** Plain text, one reply level,
   identity/audience preview, exact committed states, report/hide/restore,
   preserved drafts, deterministic containment, privacy paths, and no media or
   DMs.
6. **Add quiet operations.** Exception-first moderation, digest-oriented typed
   notification occurrences, rate limits, tenant-fair backpressure, privacy-
   safe observability, drift repair, kill switches, export, and a rehearsed
   incident path.
7. **Certify production-shaped behavior.** Test every scope substitution,
   public cache and realtime non-leakage, service-role commands, RLS owner/
   bypass behavior, stale/offline retries, report abuse, XSS/URL inputs,
   retention/export/erasure, 320 CSS-pixel reflow, keyboard/screen-reader/mobile
   behavior, and skewed-load isolation before enabling a tenant.

The resulting experience is intentionally quiet: tenants that choose off see
no response UI or moderation work; acknowledgement-only tenants get the
Epistle-style encouragement loop without comments; and comment-enabled tenants
receive one clear conversation surface plus an exception queue, not a social
platform.

### 27.6 Ratified hardened formulation

**C-prime-amended-and-hardened (C-prime-R) — one prospective, immutable,
tenant-owned Supporter Response Profile Version, initially `Responses off` and
then choosing exactly one of `Responses off`, `Like + I prayed`, or
`Like + I prayed + comments`, with acknowledgement-only recommended in guided
setup; acting only
as a ceiling over exact D11 Supporter Release Projection-bound Engagement
Spaces, each structurally carrying Tenant, Legal Entity, environment, canonical
source and purpose, Update ID and immutable Revision, Release Projection and
version, audience, safety and authorization epochs, Response Profile Version,
and operation generation; with per-update narrowing, immediate
evidence-preserving closure, and reopening only through D4/D5's existing exact
Review & Release authority. Current authenticated purpose-authorized access is
re-proved on every count, list, react, unreact, comment, reply, edit, withdraw,
report, moderate, export, stream, and notification-deep-link request before any
elevated command. Like and I prayed are two fixed, reversible, idempotent,
audience-local acknowledgements; optional comments are bounded plain text with
safe links, audience-safe identity preview, immutable self-edit revisions,
self-withdrawal and privacy-safe tombstones, one same-space reply level, keyset
pagination, and exact pending, posted, held, closed, and failed states. Enabling
comments progressively reveals one tenant-selected Right away, with reporting
or After review posture and one existing authorized moderation group; one quiet
exception-first lane provides report, reversible hold/hide/restore, immediate
source-authorized safety hiding, reasoned privacy/safety redaction, prospective
comment lock, and smallest-scope actor restriction without staff rewriting a
supporter's words. Counts are rebuildable audience-local projections, never
mutable canonical Update facts; Phase 22 emits typed, deduplicable response and
moderation occurrences only, while Phases 17/6 independently own recipient,
consent, suppression, cadence, batching, dispatch, and provider outcome and
D7/Phase 13 alone own the adjacent Give action and every checkout, gift,
settlement, and attribution fact. Anonymous Public Releases remain read-only
and contain no protected count, identity, comment, cursor, cache fragment,
metadata, hydration state, or realtime event; existing releases never change
silently; uncertain writes never appear posted; safety narrowing fails closed
at the smallest scope; and activation requires production-shaped cross-scope,
concurrency, abuse, failure, migration, privacy, accessibility, and load proof—
without public or anonymous writing, cross-audience totals, arbitrary reactions,
rich or media comments, mentions, direct messages, social graphs, unbounded
threads, gamification, donation-derived authority, trusted-user safety bypass,
AI-only judgment, raw profile/table/realtime exposure, mutable post counters as
truth, destructive ordinary deletion, hidden per-response email, blind retry,
dual write, reinterpretation of legacy demo love/prayer/fire or comment data as
certified truth, or any claim that viewed, opened, liked, prayed, commented,
notified, delivered, relationally connected, started checkout, gave, settled,
or paid are the same fact.**

The founder ratified this exact formulation as Phase 22 D12 on 2026-08-06.
See [ADR-0129](../../adr/0129-bounded-supporter-response-profiles.md) and the
[Phase 22 decision log](./phase-22-public-ministry-pages-decision-log.md#d12--what-bounded-response-experience-may-purpose-authorized-supporters-use-on-a-ministry-update).

### 27.7 Unresolved factual unknowns

The current public primary sources do not establish:

- Epistle's exact response authorization, comment visibility, moderation,
  deletion, reporting, blocking, retention, notification preference, or API
  semantics;
- whether Epistle binds responses to a particular historical post revision or
  how corrections affect an existing conversation;
- the internal consistency, audit, RLS, cache, realtime, rate-limit, or retry
  guarantees of any comparison product;
- comparison-product accessibility conformance under actual assistive
  technology, mobile zoom, reflow, latency, and failure conditions; or
- a universal legal retention period for supporter comments. Retention,
  erasure, legal hold, and export must remain jurisdiction- and tenant-policy-
  aware rather than being inferred from product marketing.

These unknowns do not block the hardened recommendation because C-prime-R does
not rely on any of them. They must not be converted into vendor-parity claims.

## 28. Unratified D13 research — safe public directory, search, and discovery

> **Status:** UNRATIFIED research and options only. This section does not
> ratify D13 and does not alter D1–D12. D12 is recorded exactly as approved in
> the decision log and ADR-0129. D2 remains authoritative for Publication Reach:
> only the current `Listed publicly` release is eligible for ordinary discovery;
> `Shared by link — public` and `Not public` releases are not.

### 28.1 Why this is the next dependency-ordered seam

D2 names **Listed publicly**, but Phase 22 has not yet defined the directory
that makes that reach useful. That omission is now load-bearing. D13 must be
settled before SEO, public metadata, analytics, cache invalidation, or
migration can say what an ordinary visitor is allowed to enumerate.

The decision is not merely whether a page appears in a grid. Search terms,
facets, result counts, sort order, map pins, pagination cursors, cache keys,
empty states, and external indexes can each reveal a person or project that the
page itself would not safely reveal. A correct page renderer cannot repair an
unsafe discovery index after the fact.

The exact founder decision is:

> **How should a tenant's currently Listed-public Missionary Ministry Pages
> and Project/Campaign Pages be browsed and searched, and which public facts
> may the directory expose or derive?**

### 28.2 Concrete scenario that the contract must resolve

Hope Mission has one English Site and one Spanish Site. Its current releases
include:

- 72 listed Missionary Ministry Pages, including six workers whose public
  identity is an approved alias and whose location is only the generalized
  Phase 10 label `Central Asia`;
- 14 listed Project/Campaign Pages, three with D6 one-time progress and eleven
  without public progress;
- five public-by-link pages intentionally omitted from normal discovery;
- one worker whose reach was just narrowed by Phase 10; and
- one project whose D7 Giving binding is temporarily ineligible while the page
  itself remains safe to read.

A donor searches `teacher`, filters to projects, opens a result, and may choose
to Give. Meanwhile, finance changes nothing, a staff editor features a project,
the Spanish translation is still missing, and the narrowed worker is present
in an old browser cache.

A safe result must include every and only current eligible release for that
exact Tenant × Legal Entity × Site × locale scope; search only approved public
facts; remove the narrowed worker without waiting for a manual directory edit;
keep the public-by-link pages absent; omit Spanish results that have no current
Spanish release rather than falling back to a legal name or English draft;
allow the project page to remain discoverable while omitting its unavailable
Give action; and never expose exact geography, internal identifiers, hidden
record counts, or the existence of a contained record.

### 28.3 Ratified boundaries inherited by D13

D13 can define discovery, but it cannot recreate or weaken the truths already
owned elsewhere:

1. **D1 owns page family, source, subject, and contributor authority.** A
   directory card does not create a page, Party, Project, contributor, or
   subject relationship.
2. **D2 owns effective reach.** Directory membership is derived from the exact
   current `Listed publicly` release. It is not a second `Show in directory`
   visibility switch. Public-by-link means hard to discover, not private, and
   remains absent from normal directories, navigation, search, sitemaps, and
   feeds.
3. **Phase 10 owns the publication ceiling and public identity/geography
   projection.** D13 may consume the admitted alias, image, summary, focus, or
   generalized region; it may not infer a safer-looking value from operational
   records.
4. **D3 owns approved presentation and typed blocks; D9 owns public media
   derivatives.** A directory card is a bounded projection, not an alternate
   editor or image pipeline.
5. **D6 owns whether and how progress is public.** A directory cannot derive a
   progress bar merely because a goal or gift exists.
6. **D7 and Phase 13 own the exact current Giving offer and checkout handoff.**
   A page can remain a valid search result when its Give action is absent or
   unavailable.
7. **D8 owns the current public route and lifecycle disposition.** Search does
   not synthesize slugs, preserve stale URLs, or override retirement.
8. **Phase 5 owns public-site runtime primitives, while Phase 22 D18 owns the
   Public Ministry semantic composition.** Phase 24 owns locale availability
   and configuration. D13 supplies the safe directory projection and query
   contract; none of them creates a second page-serving runtime.

### 28.4 Current repository evidence and contradictions

The existing routes prove a useful interaction concept but are not a safe
foundation to promote as D13 truth:

- `apps/donor/app/(public)/(hero)/workers/page.tsx` publishes a static
  `Missionary Directory` route with no Tenant, Legal Entity, Site, locale,
  release-generation, or Phase 10 projection boundary.
- `apps/donor/app/(public)/(hero)/workers/workers-client.tsx` calls the mock
  `getFieldWorkers()`, searches title, full location, and description in the
  browser, derives filter values from every row, displays an exact result
  count, and presents a `Sort: Priority` control with no corresponding sort
  implementation. It also claims a verified roster, regional coverage, and
  `100% Direct. 0% Delay.` without authoritative proof. Those are demo claims,
  not reusable product semantics.
- `packages/mock-data/index.ts` derives directory category by splitting a
  missionary's `ministryFocus`, converts monthly support into an annualized
  raised/goal pair, and exposes mock location and image data. It has no D1,
  D2, D6, D7, D8, D9, Legal Entity, Site, locale, or safety-generation proof.
- `apps/donor/app/(public)/(solid)/where-we-work/map-wrapper.tsx` groups worker,
  project, and custom-location rows in the browser, exposes exact latitude and
  longitude to four decimal places, renders exact map pins, reports aggregate
  worker/project counts, and constructs worker and checkout routes from raw
  `linked_id` values. Selection zooms the map to a local level. That is
  incompatible with the Phase 10 safety boundary for sensitive workers and
  does not provide an equivalent list-first accessible experience.
- `packages/database/hooks/public-locations.ts` reads a live client collection
  and filters only `status = 'published'`. `supabase/schema.sql` defines
  `public.locations` with nullable `tenant_id`, exact coordinates, free-form
  `type`/`linked_id`, and no Legal Entity, Site, locale, reach, release,
  route, or Phase 10 generation coordinates.
- `supabase/migrations/20260625002117_canonical_tanstack_db_realtime_rls.sql`
  grants anonymous/authenticated reads of those location rows when status is
  `published` and publishes the table through Realtime. That one-column policy
  can leak cross-tenant rows and exact geography; it cannot be grandfathered
  into D13.
- `apps/donor/app/(public)/(solid)/workers/[id]/page.tsx` statically generates
  every mock worker route and includes location in structured data. Neither
  static params nor JSON-LD is a safe substitute for current-release
  eligibility.
- `packages/lib/cms/public-page.ts` has useful public-page descriptors and
  cache policy seams, but no public directory membership/search projection.
  Its legacy payload identifiers must not become search tokens.
- Existing tests validate mock identifiers and some public-page mechanics, but
  none certifies scope substitution, hidden-field non-searchability, stale
  cursor rejection, Phase 10 narrowing, exact directory membership, or
  location/count non-leakage.

The permanent fix is replacement with an explicitly scoped public projection,
not another condition on `public.locations` and not a client-side filter over
operational or CMS records.

### 28.5 Current first-party and primary-source research

Research checked on 2026-08-06 supports a simple family-aware directory while
also showing why Asym must not copy every visible feature:

- [ABWE's Workers and Projects giving surface](https://give.abwe.org/projects)
  combines workers and projects, promotes featured projects, and connects
  discovery to `More` and `Give Now`. It validates one coherent donor journey,
  but its public interface is not evidence that country, status, newest sort,
  counts, or internal filtering inputs are safe for every tenant.
- [TEAM's Ways to Give page](https://www.team.org/ways-to-give/) gives distinct
  search entry points for US workers, short-term workers, and ministry
  projects. It validates clear family labels instead of an undifferentiated
  result pile.
- [CTEN's missionary directory](https://www.cten.org/missionaries) combines a
  name search with `Browse by Location` and visibly uses protected aliases
  such as `A and D`. This matches real missionary practice, while also proving
  that location browsing and search labels must be supplied by a safety-owned
  public projection rather than copied from a Party or address.
- [Reliant's current help page](https://reliant.org/help/website-technical/how-do-i-search-for-a-missionary-or-ministry),
  last updated in 2016, documents searches by name, ministry location, fund
  number, church name, and keywords. The discoverability goal is relevant;
  fund-number and internal-relationship search are deliberate non-patterns for
  Asym because they make operational identifiers and private associations
  public lookup keys.
- [USWDS Search](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/search/) recommends
  a visible labelled search field, retained query text, a real submit button,
  and simple search before advanced search. Its
  [Collection guidance](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/collection/)
  recommends semantic lists, concise cards, strong information scent, and
  unique link names, and directs larger catalogs to a dedicated index.
- [W3C's WCAG 2.2 status-message guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html)
  specifically treats `18 results returned` and `No results returned` as
  status updates that assistive technology must be able to announce without a
  focus jump. [WCAG 2.2 Reflow](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/reflow.html)
  requires the ordinary list/search experience to work at 320 CSS pixels; a
  map's two-dimensional exception is not permission to make a map the only
  discovery path.
- [PostgreSQL's current full-text-search documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-tables.html)
  recommends an index for practical text search, documents GIN and stored
  generated `tsvector` options, and requires an explicit matching text-search
  configuration for stable indexed behavior. This is enough for bounded
  launch search without an external search vendor.
- [Supabase's current API-security guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api)
  recommends a dedicated exposed API schema so internal tables and functions
  remain unexposed. Its
  [RLS guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)
  warns that views normally use creator privileges and therefore require
  `security_invoker = true` or removal from anonymous/authenticated exposure.
  D13 needs both structural scope and a deliberately small public API; a
  broad browser-readable table is not made safe by UI filtering.

Comparable sites validate donor expectations, not their hidden data models,
authorization, cache behavior, or accessibility conformance. No vendor's
public page was treated as proof of tenant isolation or safety.

### 28.6 Bounded product options

#### Option A-prime — Separate complete directories by page family

Publish one Missionaries directory and one Projects directory for each Site and
locale. Each directory automatically lists every current eligible release in
that family and offers a simple family-specific search. Tenant navigation may
link to either or both.

- **Strengths:** clearest mental model, lowest query/UI complexity, strong
  alignment with TEAM's separate entry points, and no cross-family result
  ambiguity.
- **Weaknesses:** duplicated landing copy and navigation, two places for donors
  to search, and poor discovery when a visitor knows the ministry topic but
  not whether its subject is a person or project.
- **Best fit:** tenants whose worker and project audiences are operationally
  distinct and who prefer separate public destinations.

#### Option B-prime — One universal directory with rich filters and a map

Publish one combined directory with result counts, free-text search, page
family, ministry focus, geography, status, progress, and other filters; offer
list and map views and tenant-selectable sort modes.

- **Strengths:** visually rich, resembles several mission-organization sites,
  and supports complex browsing for very large public catalogs.
- **Weaknesses:** largest safety and enumeration surface; exact maps and counts
  can expose restricted presence; mutable filter taxonomies become a second
  public-data system; activity/progress sorting leaks operational patterns;
  mobile, keyboard, screen-reader, cache, and query complexity are materially
  higher. It also invites adaptation of the unsafe current `locations` model.
- **Best fit:** not Phase 22. A future map would require its own Phase 10-owned
  public geography contract and a complete equivalent list experience.

#### Option C-prime — One scoped Public Ministry Directory with typed family sections and bounded search — Recommended

Publish one Site/locale landing route whose source-complete membership is
derived automatically from current D2 `Listed publicly` releases. Present
Missionary Ministry Pages and Project/Campaign Pages as clearly labelled typed
sections or tabs, with one simple search across exact approved public card
fields and an optional family filter. Hide an empty family; never mix the two
families into indistinguishable cards.

Tenants may configure the directory heading, introduction, section order, and
a bounded featured set selected only from currently eligible listed releases.
Featuring affects placement, never membership, safety, route, or Giving
eligibility. Safe focus and generalized-region filters appear only when the
tenant has enabled those code-owned public fields and they are useful; they
show no facet counts. Phase 22 launches without a map, arbitrary taxonomy
builder, external search service, newest/popularity/progress sorting, or a
second per-page directory toggle.

- **Strengths:** one understandable donor destination, clear family separation,
  near-zero per-page admin work, precise D2 semantics, and a substantially
  smaller leakage and maintenance surface than B-prime.
- **Weaknesses:** needs a real versioned projection, locale-aware search index,
  current-release invalidation, and disciplined card schema. Large tenants may
  later need additional safe facets, which must be added as explicit public
  projection fields rather than arbitrary database columns.
- **Why recommended:** it preserves the most useful pattern from ABWE and the
  clarity of TEAM while keeping Phase 10 safety, tenant isolation, and staff
  workload visible and testable.

### 28.7 Recommended UX if C-prime is selected

#### Visitor experience

1. The route opens with tenant-authored heading/intro and two plain family
   choices: **Missionaries** and **Projects**. On small catalogs they can be
   stacked headings; on larger catalogs they can be accessible tabs/filters
   backed by URL state. The family distinction is never color-only.
2. One visibly labelled **Search ministries** field and submit button searches
   only the current locale's approved public tokens. The query remains in the
   field after submission. An empty query shows the stable default catalog;
   malformed or all-stopword input returns a calm explanation, not all hidden
   matches or an error page.
3. Filters are progressive disclosure. If no meaningful safe filter exists,
   no empty filter panel is shown. Selected filters appear as removable chips
   with **Clear all**; mobile uses a labelled sheet, preserves selections, and
   returns focus predictably.
4. Results are a semantic list/grid of cards with one unique title link,
   D9's directory-card derivative or a neutral no-photo treatment, a brief
   approved summary, and only approved safe public labels. A D6 progress
   summary appears only when that exact page profile enables it. A secondary
   **Give** action appears only when D7 currently admits it; its absence does
   not imply that the ministry or page is inactive.
5. Dynamic result status (`12 ministries`, `No matching ministries`, `Search
unavailable`) is visible and politely announced. The no-result state keeps
   the query, offers **Clear search**, and never hints that withheld records
   exist.
6. Results use a stable deterministic order: tenant-featured eligible releases
   first, then a locale-appropriate stable public-title key with opaque ID as
   the final tie-breaker. There is no `Priority`, `Newest`, `Most supported`,
   `Almost funded`, popularity, random, or last-activity sort.
7. Bounded keyset pagination or **Load more** preserves the URL-scoped query and
   filters. Cursor scope includes Tenant, Legal Entity, Site, locale, page
   family, query/filter digest, sort contract, and projection generation; a
   stale or substituted cursor fails closed and restarts calmly.
8. The complete path works with keyboard, screen reader, 200% text spacing,
   320 CSS-pixel reflow, reduced motion, images disabled, and JavaScript delay
   or failure. A map is neither required nor offered at launch.

#### Tenant staff experience

The Public Pages workspace has one **Directory** setup surface per Site/locale,
not a directory checkbox on every page. Its default copy explains:
**Listed-public pages appear here automatically. Public-by-link and not-public
pages do not.** Staff can edit heading/intro, order the two families, and choose
featured pages from an eligibility-filtered picker with a live preview.

A quiet diagnostic list shows each current page as **Included** or **Not
included**, with one source-owned reason such as `Shared by link`, `No current
Spanish release`, `Safety-limited`, or `Retired`. Staff cannot override the
reason from the directory. The action links to the owning D2, D4/D5, D8, or
Phase 10 surface. Healthy tenants do not receive a directory reconciliation
queue or repeated certification task.

Safe focus/region filters stay collapsed under **Optional browsing filters**.
The UI previews exactly which public labels and cards a visitor can search.
It never exposes internal search tokens, legal names, Party IDs, Designation
IDs, fund numbers, exact coordinates, or hidden-record counts.

### 28.8 Recommended domain and database boundary

If selected, C-prime should use one rebuildable **Public Ministry Directory
Projection**, not query operational tables from the browser:

- Every row is structurally scoped to exact Tenant, Legal Entity, environment,
  Site, locale, Page Family, Public Page, immutable current Release, D2 reach
  version, D8 route generation, Phase 10 safety/admission generation, and
  projection generation. Same-scope foreign keys/constraints prevent a card,
  media derivative, progress summary, or route from crossing coordinates.
- Membership is computed from a complete release census. Exactly one current
  eligible directory row exists for each current listed release. A
  public-by-link, not-public, withdrawn, contained, retired, missing-locale, or
  ambiguous release has no row. An exclusion is recorded privately with its
  source-owned reason for staff diagnostics, not returned as a public placeholder.
- The public row contains only a stable opaque page identifier, current public
  route, family, public title/alias, approved short summary, D9 card derivative,
  optional D6-owned presentation, optional D7 action capability, code-owned
  safe public labels, stable sort keys, and explicit as-of/generation facts.
  It contains no legal name, internal alias, Party/worker/fund/Designation
  lookup key, operational notes, exact location, employment/support status,
  donor count, hidden-result count, or raw CMS document.
- Search tokens are generated only from those exact public fields. Launch uses
  PostgreSQL full-text search with an explicitly pinned configuration per
  supported locale and a matching GIN/generated-vector strategy. Unsupported
  locale behavior is declared and tested; it never silently searches a
  different locale or hidden source. Fuzzy/phonetic search, arbitrary tenant
  synonyms, and an external index are deferred.
- Internal canonical/projection tables remain in an unexposed schema. The
  anonymous API is a bounded read command or deliberately narrow
  `security_invoker` projection with explicit grants and scope filters. No raw
  table or Realtime publication is the public contract; client-side filtering
  is presentation only.
- Reads bind membership, query, count, cards, and next cursor to one projection
  generation so a page cannot count one snapshot and render another. Build and
  invalidation are idempotent. Phase 10 narrowing or D2/D8 change removes the
  affected positive row first or atomically; failures preserve authorized
  negative/contained behavior and never fall back to mock, Payload, Party,
  designation, or `locations` data.
- Cache keys and tags carry the same public scope and generation. Tenant-fair
  query limits, input-length limits, timeouts, and pagination bounds prevent
  one catalog or abusive wildcard search from degrading other tenants.
- Phase 22 emits typed directory projection/rebuild/invalidation occurrences;
  future SEO or external-search consumers must independently prove current D2
  and Phase 10 authority. Search-engine removal is not proof that the Asym
  directory is safe, and directory removal is not proof of external de-indexing.

### 28.9 Ruthless risk preview

| Concern                                   | What could go wrong and why it matters                                                                                          | Severity    | Likelihood before hardening           | Permanent prevention                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Hidden-record enumeration                 | Counts, facets, timing, autocomplete, or different error messages reveal people/projects that are not listed.                   | Critical    | High                                  | Index only the current public projection; return no hidden-match metadata; use indistinguishable public absence and fixed bounded responses.                           |
| Cross-tenant/Site/locale leakage          | A broad `published` predicate, nullable scope, cursor substitution, or cache collision returns another tenant's card.           | Critical    | High in the current `locations` shape | Structural non-null scope, same-scope constraints, narrow API, RLS/command reproof, generation-bound caches/cursors, adversarial scope-substitution tests.             |
| Safety/location disclosure                | Full addresses, exact pins, country facets, legal names, image metadata, or structured data expose a restricted worker.         | Critical    | High if the current map is reused     | Phase 10-owned public labels only; no launch map; D9 derivatives; inspect HTML, JSON, cache, analytics, and accessibility trees for hidden values.                     |
| Stale positive discovery                  | A narrowed or retired page remains in a cache, browser collection, Realtime event, or search index.                             | Critical    | Medium–high                           | Positive-row removal/containment first, short bounded cache plus tagged invalidation, generation fences, synthetic stale-consumer tests, no raw Realtime subscription. |
| Duplicate/conflicting visibility controls | Staff hide a directory card while D2 says listed, or expose it while D2 says public-by-link.                                    | High        | High if a page-level toggle is added  | Directory membership is fully derived from D2; staff diagnostics route corrections to the owning surface.                                                              |
| Misleading Giving or progress             | Search ranking or cards imply urgency, availability, current support, or a valid Give route when source truth changed.          | High        | Medium                                | D6/D7 capability projection only; omit unavailable optional facts; no progress/popularity ranking; label through-date where shown.                                     |
| Search-language brittleness               | One English tokenizer makes names or summaries in another locale unfindable or inconsistent after restore.                      | Medium–high | Medium                                | Explicit locale/config contract, matching indexed/query configuration, fixtures for diacritics and non-Latin text, declared unsupported behavior.                      |
| Accessibility and mobile failure          | Live filtering is silent, focus jumps, filter drawers trap users, cards have duplicate link names, or the map is the only path. | High        | High in custom rich-filter UIs        | Server/URL-backed baseline, labelled controls, polite result status, unique links, semantic lists, reflow/zoom/AT testing, no required map.                            |
| Scalability/noisy tenants                 | Browser filtering, unindexed text, OFFSET scans, huge result hydration, or wildcard queries become slow and unfair.             | High        | Medium                                | GIN-backed bounded query, keyset pagination, maximum query/result bounds, tenant-fair rate/concurrency limits, representative skewed-load tests.                       |
| Operational burden                        | Staff manually map every page, repair stale rows, curate taxonomies, or certify each release.                                   | High        | Medium                                | Complete automatic membership, bounded optional feature list, disposable projection, exception-only diagnostics, idempotent rebuild and reconciliation.                |
| External-index coupling                   | A future search vendor becomes a second visibility authority or retains withdrawn pages.                                        | Critical    | Medium if introduced early            | No external vendor at launch; later adapter consumes only versioned public projection, proves delete/tombstone behavior, and never controls reach.                     |

### 28.10 Proof required before any launch implementation may be accepted

A later spec must make at least these observable tests mandatory:

1. complete membership and zero extras across listed, public-by-link,
   not-public, draft, withdrawn, contained, retired, and missing-locale releases;
2. exhaustive Tenant × Legal Entity × environment × Site × locale × family ×
   release/safety-generation substitution against reads, counts, filters,
   cards, cursors, caches, structured responses, and service-role commands;
3. proof that legal names, internal aliases, operational notes, exact
   coordinates, fund/Party/Designation IDs, hidden counts, and unpublished
   media never affect a match or appear in HTML, JSON, RSC payloads, logs,
   analytics, error text, cache keys visible to clients, accessibility trees,
   or Realtime;
4. concurrent release replacement, Phase 10 narrowing, D2 reach change,
   retirement, projection rebuild, stale cursor, retry, and cache failure with
   affected-positive-only containment and no raw-source fallback;
5. locale fixtures for accents, punctuation, aliases, non-Latin scripts,
   empty/all-stopword input, long/adversarial input, stable order, and
   pagination without duplicates or omissions;
6. D6/D7 degradation proving a readable page stays discoverable when optional
   progress or Give is absent, while an invalid route/current release does not;
7. keyboard, screen-reader, focus, status announcement, 320 CSS-pixel reflow,
   zoom, text spacing, reduced-motion, image-failure, no-JavaScript baseline,
   slow-network, and mobile touch-target validation; and
8. representative large and highly skewed tenant catalogs, abusive query
   traffic, rebuild load, and tenant-fair backpressure with observable lag,
   failure reason, reconciliation, and safe recovery.

### 28.11 Founder question — one decision only

Which Phase 22 public discovery contract should Asym adopt?

- **A-prime:** separate complete Missionary and Project directories;
- **B-prime:** one rich universal directory with filters and a map; or
- **C-prime (recommended):** one Site/locale-scoped Public Ministry Directory
  with automatic D2-listed membership, typed Missionary and Project sections,
  bounded safe search/filtering, tenant-configurable presentation/featuring,
  and no map or second visibility switch at launch?

No Phase 22 D13 decision is recorded by this section.

## 29. Ratified D13 adversarial review — one authority, tenant-chosen directory topology

> **Status:** accepted as the binding Phase 22 D13 founder ruling on 2026-08-06
> after adversarial review. The exact §29.3 formulation is ratified without
> changing D1–D12.

### 29.1 Ruthless verdict

The amendment makes product sense, but a literal implementation of “separate
directories or search functions” would be unsafe. Two independently configured
catalogs, indexes, or membership rules would drift and eventually expose an
ineligible worker, omit a listed project, or return the wrong Tenant, Legal
Entity, Site, locale, or Page Family. Tenant flexibility must therefore stop at
the **presentation topology**.

Asym should expose exactly two mutually exclusive public layouts for each exact
Tenant × Legal Entity × Site × locale scope:

1. **Together — recommended default.** One **Find ministries** destination with
   clearly typed Missionaries and Projects sections and one **Search
   ministries** form.
2. **Separate by family.** One canonical Missionaries destination with **Search
   missionaries** and one canonical Projects destination with **Search
   projects**.

Both layouts are views over one complete D2/Phase 10-admitted membership
projection, one query implementation, one family-typed card contract, one
generation and cache authority, and one staff setup. A separate route supplies
an immutable server-owned family constraint; it does not create a second index
or accept a client-supplied scope as authority. D2 remains the only ordinary
discovery switch: a current `Listed publicly` release is included and a
`Shared by link — public`, `Not public`, missing-locale, contained, withdrawn,
or retired release is not. Staff cannot contradict that result from Directory
settings.

### 29.2 Current evidence and modern comparator check

The market supports both public information architectures:

- [ABWE](https://give.abwe.org/projects?country=Uganda) uses a combined
  **Workers and Projects** finder with a Type filter.
- [Village Missions](https://give.villagemissions.org/) exposes separate **Find
  a Missionary** and **Find a Project** entry points.
- [Church of God World Missions](https://www.cogwm.org/give/) and [Christ for
  the City International](https://cfci.org/missions/) use combined
  missionary/project discovery.
- [Reliant](https://reliant.org/help/website-technical/how-do-i-search-for-a-missionary-or-ministry)
  demonstrates the donor expectation that one simple search can find either a
  missionary or a ministry. Its fund-number search is not a pattern Asym should
  copy because internal identifiers must not become public discovery tokens.
- [CTEN](https://www.cten.org/missionaries) demonstrates searchable aliases and
  generalized serving locations. In Asym, even those fields must come only from
  the Phase 10-approved public projection.

The UX and platform evidence points to one bounded implementation:

- [USWDS Search](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/search/) recommends
  a real labelled search form, persistent query terms, a submit button, and
  simple search before advanced search. [USWDS Collection](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/collection/)
  recommends semantic lists, concise metadata, and unique descriptive title
  links.
- [WCAG 2.2 status-message guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html)
  requires dynamic result and no-result messages to be programmatically
  announced without needlessly moving focus. [WCAG reflow guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/reflow.html)
  requires the experience to remain usable at 320 CSS pixels.
- [Shopify Search & Discovery](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-store/storefront-search/search-and-discovery-filters)
  shows filters only when applicable to the current collection or result set.
  Asym must go further for restricted ministry safety: use only explicitly
  admitted public fields and show no hidden-record facet counts.
- [Google's current faceted-navigation guidance](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/faceted-navigation)
  warns that filter parameters can create an effectively unbounded URL space
  and consume crawl and server capacity. [Google canonicalization guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization)
  also treats sorting and filtering variants as a common duplicate-content
  source. Only the active base topology belongs in ordinary navigation and the
  sitemap; query/filter states are not alternate directory authorities.
- [PostgreSQL full-text search guidance](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch-tables.html)
  supports a generated `tsvector` plus GIN index and requires an explicit text
  search configuration for a reliable indexed expression. A locale must pin
  that configuration or an explicitly declared literal-token mode.
- [Supabase API security guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/securing-your-api)
  requires grants and RLS together and recommends a dedicated exposed API
  schema while internal objects remain unexposed. [Supabase RLS guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)
  also warns that ordinary views can bypass underlying RLS unless deliberately
  protected.
- [OWASP API1:2023](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/)
  requires object authorization on every endpoint using a client-supplied
  identifier. A family, Site, locale, cursor, or page ID from a request can
  never establish its own authority.

The present repository is migration input, not a usable D13 seam:

- `apps/donor/app/(public)/(hero)/workers/workers-client.tsx` loads the complete
  mock `getFieldWorkers()` corpus into the browser, searches full location and
  description strings, derives region facets client-side, displays exact
  counts, and presents an unexplained `Priority` sort plus unsupported `100%
Direct. 0% Delay.` copy.
- `apps/donor/app/(public)/(solid)/workers/[id]/page.tsx` statically enumerates
  mock workers; stale static generation cannot become current publication or
  safety authority.
- `public.locations` has nullable `tenant_id`, exact latitude/longitude, and a
  free-form `linked_id`; the current hook filters only `status = 'published'`
  in a browser live query. Existing grants and Realtime publication make it an
  especially dangerous source for a public ministry directory.
- Current GitHub work for Site scope, Phase 5 public isolation, Phase 10 safety,
  and public projection invalidation remains independently owned and in part
  open or blocked. D13 must consume their proved contracts, not claim that a
  directory profile completes them.

### 29.3 Ratified exact hardened formulation

> **C-prime-amended-and-hardened (C-prime-R) — one versioned, exact Tenant,
> Legal Entity, environment, Site, and locale-scoped Public Ministry Discovery
> Profile choosing exactly one active presentation topology—Together by quiet
> built-in default or tenant-selected Separate by Page Family—over one
> source-complete, generation-bound Public Ministry Directory Projection, one
> bounded server query contract, and one family-typed public card contract.
> Membership is derived only from the exact current D2 `Listed publicly` Page
> Release after current Phase 10 ceiling and containment proof; combined and
> separate presentations never create independent membership, index, search,
> cache, card, or inclusion authority, and every separate route applies its
> family constraint server-side. The projection preserves exact release,
> reach, safety, route, media, optional progress, optional Giving-capability,
> profile, locale, source, coverage, and as-of generations while exposing and
> indexing only approved public card fields; it uses deterministic ordering,
> explicitly pinned locale search behavior, bounded allowlisted filters without
> hidden facet counts, tenant-fair limits, generation-bound opaque keyset
> cursors and cache keys, complete-cohort shadow rebuilds, atomic current-head
> activation, and affected-positive-first adverse removal. One accessible,
> quiet Directory setup lets staff choose Together or Separate, preview exact
> routes, labels, cards, mobile behavior, current included pages, and privately
> explained source-owned exclusions, while Listed pages enter automatically and
> healthy tenants perform no page-by-page maintenance. Visitors receive
> scope-honest labelled GET search, persistent queries, semantic typed results,
> polite status messages, stable empty/error states, and optional D6 progress
> or D7 Give actions only by current reference; a topology change alters neither
> page reach nor safety, review, content, progress, Giving, external indexing,
> or removal truth. Phase 5 remains authoritative for public request resolution,
> D8-compatible route dispositions and one non-conflicting canonical/sitemap
> manifest govern topology changes, and external crawler removal remains an
> observed best-effort outcome—without concurrent combined and separate
> catalogs, a second visibility switch, per-page directory toggles, client-side
> scope or filtering authority, raw operational/CMS/`locations` reads,
> anonymous raw tables or Realtime, separate family indexes, arbitrary search
> fields, taxonomy or query DSLs, predictive autocomplete, fuzzy or hidden
> synonym expansion, maps or exact coordinates, hidden-result placeholders or
> counts, popularity/financial/progress/urgency ranking, OFFSET pagination,
> unsafe locale or source fallback, mutable current rows, destructive rebuild,
> dual-read migration, or any claim that released, listed, searchable,
> Giving-ready, externally indexed, locally removed, and externally de-indexed
> are the same fact.**

### 29.4 Exact UX contract

#### Tenant staff

Directory setup is one surface under the exact Site and locale, not a matrix and
not a setting on every page. A vertical two-choice fieldset says:

- **Together — recommended:** `Supporters search missionaries and projects from
one page. Results remain clearly separated.`
- **Separate pages:** `Supporters use a Missionaries page and a Projects page,
each with its own search.`

The same screen previews the exact public URLs and navigation labels, desktop
and mobile composition, current eligible public cards, and a private diagnostic
summary of included and excluded releases. It states plainly that the choice
does **not** change page reach, Phase 10 safety, review, progress, or Giving.
Exclusions carry one source-owned reason and deep-link to the owning D2, D4/D5,
D8, Phase 10, locale, or route surface; Directory settings cannot override the
reason. Activation is blocked only by actionable route collision, missing
locale contract, incomplete membership, stale safety/reach evidence, or invalid
canonical/sitemap proof. Healthy tenants never recertify every page.

#### Visitors and donors

- Together uses **Search ministries** and visibly typed Missionaries and
  Projects sections. Separate pages use **Search missionaries** or **Search
  projects**; a query can never silently broaden across families.
- Search is a normal URL-backed GET form with a persistent value and explicit
  submit. The base catalog and page navigation work without client JavaScript.
  Predictive autocomplete is out of scope at launch.
- Only useful, code-owned, Phase 10-approved generalized-region or ministry-
  focus filters appear. They use progressive disclosure on small screens, show
  no hidden facet counts, have a visible **Clear all**, and preserve focus.
- Results are semantic lists/grids. Every card has a unique linked public title,
  visible Page Family, D9-approved card derivative or neutral no-photo state,
  brief approved summary, and only admitted public labels. D6 progress and a
  distinct D7 Give action appear only when their current independent authority
  admits them.
- Result count, no-match, loading completion, and search failure are visible
  and politely announced. No-match retains the query and offers **Clear
  search**. No state says or implies that withheld records exist.
- Together hides an empty family section. Separate keeps its configured family
  URL stable with a neutral `No public projects are available right now` style
  state, omits the empty family from ordinary navigation/index signals, and
